lessons.title: What is Smali?
lessons.summary: Smali is the human-readable assembly language for Dalvik bytecode, the instruction set stored in the classes.dex files of every Android app. Learn where it comes from, how it relates to Java and Kotlin, and how to read your first method.

sections.title: From source code to Smali
sections.body:
When you build an Android app, the Java or Kotlin compiler first produces ordinary JVM .class files. The Android build tools (today the D8 dexer, with R8 for release builds) then translate those classes into Dalvik bytecode and pack them into one or more classes.dex files inside the APK.

Dalvik bytecode is a binary format, so it is hard to read directly. Smali is a text syntax for it:
every Dalvik instruction, class, field and method has a one-to-one textual form. The name comes from the Icelandic word for "assembler"; its companion tool baksmali ("disassembler") turns a .dex file back into .smali text files, one per class.

sections.title: Why learn it?
sections.body:
Because Smali maps directly to the bytecode, it shows exactly what the device will execute:
- which registers hold which values,
- which methods are called and with which arguments,
- how branches, loops and exception handlers are laid out.

That precision is why Smali is the language of choice when you need to understand how a compiled app behaves, debug a build or optimisation problem, or study what the compiler generated for your own code.

sections.title: A complete Smali class
Equivalent Java
Reading the listing
sections.body:
Read the listing from top to bottom. Lines starting with a dot are directives: .class names the class using a type descriptor (Lcom/acme/demo/Greeter;), .super names its superclass, and .method ... .end method wraps one method. The method header greet(Ljava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String; says it takes one String and returns a String.

Inside the method, .registers 3 reserves three registers. The single argument arrives in the last one, which Smali also lets you call p0 because the method is static. Every other line is one instruction: create a StringBuilder, call its constructor, load a constant string, call append twice, call toString, copy the result into v0 with move-result-object and return it.
Smali is not a decompiler output. A decompiler guesses Java source; Smali shows the real instructions. When a decompiled view looks odd, the Smali is the ground truth.

sections.title: Use it responsibly
sections.body: Only analyse apps you wrote yourself or are explicitly authorised to examine. Respect licences, terms of service and the law in your country.

exercises.prompt: Write a static method answer()I in a class Lcom/acme/demo/Quiz; that returns the number 42. Use as few registers as possible.
exercises.solution:
.class public Lcom/acme/demo/Quiz;
.super Ljava/lang/Object;

.method public static answer()I
    .registers 1
    const/16 v0, 0x2a
    return v0
.end method
exercises.hint: 42 does not fit in the 4-bit literal of const/4 (range -8..7), but it fits in const/16.

exercises.prompt: In the Greeter example, which instruction stores the value returned by toString() into a register, and why is it needed?
exercises.solution:
move-result-object v0 copies the object returned by the immediately preceding invoke-virtual
into v0. Invoke instructions never write a register themselves; the result must be fetched by
a move-result* instruction placed directly after the call.
exercises.hint: Look at the line right after the last invoke-virtual.

quiz.question: What does Smali represent?
options: A text syntax for Dalvik bytecode stored in .dex files
A decompiled approximation of the original Java source
The machine code ART generates for ARM CPUs
A scripting language that runs inside Android apps
quiz.explanation: Smali is an assembly-style, one-to-one textual form of Dalvik bytecode. Decompilers produce Java-like guesses; ART's AOT output is native machine code, which is a different thing.

quiz.question: Which tool turns a classes.dex file into .smali text files?
quiz.explanation: baksmali disassembles .dex into .smali; smali assembles .smali back into .dex.

quiz.question: What does this line declare?
quiz.explanation: .super names the direct superclass. Every class except java.lang.Object has exactly one.

quiz.question: Why does the Greeter example need move-result-object after calling toString()?
options: Invoke instructions do not write their result to a register
To convert the String into a primitive
Because toString() is a static method
It releases the StringBuilder for garbage collection
quiz.explanation: An invoke stores its return value in a hidden result slot. move-result, move-result-wide or move-result-object must immediately follow the call to copy it into a register.

lessons.title: The Android Runtime
lessons.summary: Dalvik bytecode is executed by the Android Runtime (ART), which replaced the original Dalvik virtual machine. See how interpretation, JIT and ahead-of-time compilation fit together, and why the bytecode you read in Smali remains the contract between an app and the device.

sections.title: From Dalvik to ART
sections.body:
Early Android versions ran apps on the Dalvik virtual machine. Dalvik interpreted bytecode and, from Android 2.2, added a just-in-time (JIT) compiler that translated frequently executed code into native instructions while the app was running.

Android 4.4 shipped the Android Runtime (ART) as a developer option, and Android 5.0 made it the only runtime. ART and Dalvik execute the same DEX bytecode, so an app built for one runs on the other; what changed is how and when that bytecode turns into machine code.

sections.title: Interpreter, JIT and AOT
sections.body:
ART can run a method in three ways:
- Interpreted: the bytecode is executed instruction by instruction.
- JIT compiled: hot methods are compiled to native code at run time and kept in a code cache.
- AOT compiled: the on-device dex2oat tool compiles DEX files to native code ahead of time and stores the result in OAT files next to the app.

Android 5.0 and 6.0 compiled almost the whole app with dex2oat at install time, which made installs and system updates slow. Android 7.0 introduced a hybrid model: apps start out interpreted and JIT-compiled, the JIT records which methods are hot in a profile, and later, when the device is idle and charging, dex2oat compiles just those methods (the speed-profile filter). Play Store cloud profiles and Baseline Profiles shipped inside apps let this happen even before first use.

sections.title: A hot loop: interpreted first, compiled later
sections.body:
.method public static sum([I)I
    .registers 4

    const/4 v0, 0x0          # total
    const/4 v1, 0x0          # index

    :loop
    array-length v2, p0
    if-ge v1, v2, :done
    aget v2, p0, v1
    add-int/2addr v0, v2
    add-int/lit8 v1, v1, 0x1
    goto :loop

    :done
    return v0
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
What this means for Smali readers
sections.body:
Whichever execution mode ART picks, it must produce the same observable behaviour as the bytecode. Native code from the JIT or dex2oat is a cache that can be thrown away and regenerated; the DEX bytecode is the real program. That is why reading Smali tells you what an app does, regardless of the device, Android version or compilation state.

Before any of this happens, ART verifies each class: it checks that registers are used with consistent types, that branches land on instruction boundaries and that method and field references make sense. Bytecode that fails verification is rejected, typically with a java.lang.VerifyError when the class is used.

On a test device with your own debuggable app you can trigger profile-guided compilation with adb shell cmd package compile -m speed-profile -f <package>, or drop the compiled code by using -m verify instead (the app then runs interpreted and JIT-compiled again). This is handy for reproducing performance issues.

sections.title: Dalvik-era assumptions
sections.body: Tricks that relied on Dalvik quirks, such as editing bytecode in memory or depending on tolerated-but-invalid DEX files, often break on ART because its verifier and compiler are stricter.

exercises.prompt: Write a static method count([Ljava/lang/Object;)I that returns the length of the array it receives. Use .registers so that the argument ends up in p0.
exercises.starterCode:
.method public static count([Ljava/lang/Object;)I
    .registers 2
    # return the array length
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method public static count([Ljava/lang/Object;)I
    .registers 2
    array-length v0, p0
    return v0
.end method
exercises.hint: array-length vA, vB writes the length of the array in vB into vA.

exercises.prompt: An app runs slowly right after installation but gets faster after a few days of use, without an update. Using the ART execution modes, explain what most likely happened.
exercises.solution:
At first the app was interpreted and JIT-compiled on demand. The JIT recorded the hot methods
in a profile, and during idle maintenance dex2oat compiled those methods ahead of time with the
speed-profile filter. Later launches run that native code directly instead of warming up again.
exercises.hint: Think about which component writes the profile and which one reads it.

quiz.question: Which Android release made ART the only runtime, replacing Dalvik?
quiz.explanation: Android 4.4 offered ART as a developer option; Android 5.0 removed Dalvik and made ART the default and only runtime.

quiz.question: What is dex2oat?
options: The on-device tool that compiles DEX bytecode into native code ahead of time
A desktop tool that converts .class files into .dex files
The JIT compiler that runs inside the app process
A command that converts Smali text into DEX
quiz.explanation: dex2oat runs on the device and turns DEX files into OAT files containing compiled code. The desktop .class-to-.dex step is done by D8/R8, and Smali-to-DEX by the smali assembler.

quiz.question: Since Android 7.0, what typically drives which methods dex2oat compiles?
options: A profile of hot methods recorded while the app runs
Every method is always compiled at install time
quiz.explanation: The hybrid model records hot methods in a profile; background dexopt then compiles them with the speed-profile filter. Cloud and Baseline Profiles can supply that information up front.

quiz.question: ART has compiled this method to native code. Which statement is true?
quiz.code:
.method public static twice(I)I
    .registers 2
    add-int v0, p0, p0
    return v0
.end method
options: Its behaviour must still match the bytecode, so the Smali stays an accurate description
The bytecode is deleted from the APK after compilation
The native code may behave differently from the bytecode
The method can no longer be verified
quiz.explanation: Compiled code is an optimisation of the bytecode and must preserve its semantics. The DEX file inside the APK is unchanged, so reading the Smali still tells you what the method does.

quiz.question: What usually happens when a class contains bytecode that fails ART's verifier?
options: A java.lang.VerifyError is thrown when the class is used
ART silently skips the invalid instructions
The instructions are executed by the old Dalvik VM instead
quiz.explanation: Hard verification failures cause the class to be rejected, which surfaces as a VerifyError. There is no fallback to Dalvik on modern devices.

lessons.title: Dalvik Bytecode
lessons.summary: Dalvik bytecode is register-based and built from 16-bit code units. Compare it with JVM stack bytecode, tour the main instruction families and learn what the verifier checks before code is allowed to run.

sections.title: Registers instead of a stack
sections.body:
The Java virtual machine uses a stack machine: instructions push values onto an operand stack and pop them off again. Dalvik was designed as a register machine instead. Each method declares a fixed number of virtual registers, and instructions name their source and destination registers explicitly.

For c = a + b with int parameters, javac emits four stack instructions:
- iload_0 (push a)
- iload_1 (push b)
- iadd (pop both, push the sum)
- istore_2 (pop the sum into local c)

Dalvik needs a single instruction, add-int, that reads two registers and writes a third. Register code has fewer instructions to dispatch and maps well onto real CPU registers, at the cost of slightly larger individual instructions.

sections.title: c = a + b in Dalvik bytecode
sections.body:
.method public static add(II)I
    .registers 3

    # v0 = p0 + p1  (p0 is v1, p1 is v2)
    add-int v0, p0, p1
    return v0
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
Code units and formats
sections.body:
Dalvik code is a sequence of 16-bit code units. The low byte of an instruction's first unit is its opcode; the remaining bits and any following units hold registers, literals and indexes. Short instructions such as const/4 v0, 0x1 or return v0 fit in one unit, add-int needs two, a call such as invoke-virtual needs three, and const-wide with a full 64-bit literal needs five.

Each layout has a format id such as 11n, 23x or 35c. The first digit is the size in code units, the second is the number of registers, and the letter describes any extra data (n for a small literal, x for none, c for a constant-pool index). Branch offsets are also measured in code units, not bytes.

sections.title: Instruction families
sections.body:
A little over 200 opcode values are assigned, and they fall into a few families:
- Moves and constants: move, move-object, move-result*, const*, const-string, const-class.
- Arithmetic and conversion: add-int, mul-long, div-double, int-to-long, neg-float and friends.
- Objects and arrays: new-instance, new-array, check-cast, instance-of, aget/aput, array-length.
- Fields: iget/iput for instance fields, sget/sput for static fields.
- Calls: invoke-virtual, invoke-super, invoke-direct, invoke-static, invoke-interface.
- Control flow: goto, if-* comparisons, packed-switch, sparse-switch, return*, throw. Most families have typed variants (-wide for long/double, -object for references, -boolean and others for small primitives), because the verifier must know what kind of value each register holds.

sections.title: What the verifier checks
sections.body: Before ART runs a method, the verifier walks every path through it. It checks that each register holds a value of a consistent type, that a register is written before it is read, that branch targets are real instruction boundaries and that move-result follows an invoke. If you hand-edit Smali and get a VerifyError, one of these rules is usually broken.

exercises.prompt: Write a static method mul(II)I that multiplies its two int arguments and returns the product, using a single arithmetic instruction.
exercises.starterCode:
.method public static mul(II)I
    .registers 3
    # multiply p0 by p1 and return the result
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method public static mul(II)I
    .registers 3
    mul-int v0, p0, p1
    return v0
.end method
exercises.hint: The three-register form is mul-int vAA, vBB, vCC.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite the add method so it uses only two registers in total, storing the result back into the first parameter register, and still returns a + b.
exercises.starterCode:
.method public static add(II)I
    .registers 2
    # p0 is v0, p1 is v1
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method public static add(II)I
    .registers 2
    add-int/2addr p0, p1
    return p0
.end method
exercises.hint: The /2addr variants use the first register as both a source and the destination.

quiz.question: How does Dalvik bytecode pass values between instructions?
options: Through numbered virtual registers named in each instruction
Through an operand stack, like JVM bytecode
Through CPU registers chosen by the app developer
quiz.explanation: Dalvik is a register machine: each method has a fixed register frame, and instructions name the registers they read and write.

quiz.question: How big is a Dalvik code unit?
quiz.explanation: Instructions are made of one or more 16-bit code units, and branch offsets count code units.

quiz.question: In the format id 35c used by invoke-virtual, what does the 3 mean?
options: The instruction is three code units long
quiz.explanation: The first digit is the length in code units and the second is the maximum register count, so 35c is three units long, takes up to five registers and carries a constant-pool index.

quiz.question: Which family does this instruction belong to?
quiz.explanation: iget-object reads an object-typed instance field (the i stands for instance). Static fields use sget*, arrays use aget*.

quiz.question: Why do many instructions come in variants such as -wide and -object?
options: The verifier needs to know the kind of value each register holds
They are only kept for Dalvik compatibility and behave identically
They select which CPU core runs the instruction
quiz.explanation: Typed variants tell the verifier and the runtime whether a register holds a 32-bit primitive, a 64-bit pair or a reference, which matters for type safety and garbage collection.

lessons.title: DEX Files
lessons.summary: A .dex file packs all of an app's classes into shared tables of strings, types, prototypes, fields and methods. Learn what lives inside, why large apps are split into classes2.dex and beyond, and how baksmali turns a DEX file into a tree of .smali files.

sections.title: One file, many classes
sections.body:
A JVM .class file holds exactly one class. A DEX file holds many classes at once and shares their constant data: every string, type name, method prototype, field reference and method reference is stored once in a table and referred to by index. This makes DEX files compact and fast to map into memory.

At a conceptual level a DEX file contains:
- a header with the magic value, checksums, file size and the location of every table,
- id tables: string_ids, type_ids, proto_ids, field_ids, method_ids,
- class_defs describing each class defined in the file,
- a data area with the actual bytecode, string contents, annotations and debug info,
- a map_list summarising every section.

sections.title: Magic and version
sections.body: Every DEX file starts with 8 magic bytes: the text dex, a newline, a three-digit format version and a zero byte, for example dex\n035\0. Version 035 is the classic format; 037 arrived with Android 7.0 (default interface methods), 038 with Android 8.0 (invoke-polymorphic and invoke-custom), 039 with Android 9 (const-method-handle and const-method-type) and 040 with Android 10. Tools such as D8 pick the lowest version that supports the features your code uses and your minSdk.

sections.title: Every reference here becomes a table entry
sections.body:
.class public Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;
.super Ljava/lang/Object;
.source "Counter.java"

.field private count:I

.method public increment()V
    .registers 2

    iget v0, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->count:I
    add-int/lit8 v0, v0, 0x1
    iput v0, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->count:I
    return-void
.end method

sections.title: Indexes behind the names
sections.body: In the listing above, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter; is stored once in type_ids, the name count once in string_ids, and Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->count:I once in field_ids. Both iget and iput carry the same 16-bit field index. Smali shows you the resolved names so you never have to read the indexes yourself.

sections.title: The 64K reference limit and multidex
sections.body:
Instructions such as invoke-virtual refer to methods with a 16-bit index, so one DEX file can reference at most 65,536 methods. This counts every method referenced, including framework and library methods your code calls, not only the methods you define. The same limit applies to field and type references.

Larger apps are split into several files named classes.dex, classes2.dex, classes3.dex and so on. ART (Android 5.0 and later) loads all of them natively; older Dalvik devices needed the multidex support library.

sections.title: Where the .smali files go
sections.body: baksmali writes one .smali file per class and turns the package into folders: Lcom/acme/demo/Counter; becomes com/acme/demo/Counter.smali and the inner class Lcom/acme/demo/Counter$Snapshot; becomes com/acme/demo/Counter$Snapshot.smali. apktool places classes.dex in smali/ and classesN.dex in smali_classesN/.

exercises.prompt: Add a method reset()V to the Counter class that sets count back to zero. Reuse the existing field reference.
exercises.starterCode:
.method public reset()V
    .registers 2
    # store 0 into this.count
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method public reset()V
    .registers 2
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    iput v0, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->count:I
    return-void
.end method
exercises.hint: Load 0 with const/4, then write it with iput using p0 (this) as the object register.

exercises.prompt: baksmali produced the file smali_classes2/org/demo/net/Client$Builder.smali. Write the class descriptor of that class and say which DEX file it came from.
exercises.solution:
The descriptor is Lorg/demo/net/Client$Builder; (an inner class Builder of
org.demo.net.Client). Because it sits in smali_classes2, it was disassembled from classes2.dex.
exercises.hint: Folders become package segments separated by slashes; the $ marks a nested class.

quiz.question: How does a DEX file differ from a JVM .class file?
options: It holds many classes that share string, type and member tables
It holds exactly one class, like a .class file
It stores native ARM code instead of bytecode
quiz.explanation: A DEX file bundles many classes and deduplicates their constants into shared id tables, which keeps the file small.

quiz.question: What do the first bytes of a DEX file look like?
options: dex, a newline, a three-digit version and a zero byte
PK followed by a zip header
The class name of the first class
quiz.explanation: The magic is dex\n followed by a version such as 035 or 039 and a terminating zero byte. 0xCAFEBABE is the JVM class file magic, and PK starts zip archives such as APKs.

quiz.question: What does the 64K limit of a single DEX file count?
options: Method references, including methods from libraries and the framework
Only methods defined in the app's own classes
quiz.explanation: Method references are addressed with a 16-bit index, so at most 65,536 distinct methods can be referenced, whoever defines them.

quiz.question: Which path does baksmali use for this class?
quiz.explanation: Package segments become folders and the simple name, including the $1 of an anonymous class, becomes the file name with a .smali extension.

quiz.question: Which DEX format version first added invoke-polymorphic and invoke-custom?
quiz.explanation: Version 038 (Android 8.0) introduced invoke-polymorphic and invoke-custom along with method handle data. 037 added default methods, and 039 added const-method-handle and const-method-type.

lessons.title: Classes
lessons.summary: Every .smali file describes one class. Learn the header directives .class, .super, .source and .implements, how access flags such as public, final, abstract, interface and enum are written, and how nested and anonymous classes are named.

sections.title: The class header
sections.body:
A Smali file starts with a short header:
- .class with the access flags and the class descriptor, e.g. .class public final Lcom/acme/demo/User;
- .super with exactly one superclass descriptor (Ljava/lang/Object; when nothing else is extended),
- optionally .source with the original file name, used in stack traces,
- zero or more .implements lines, one per interface.

After the header come fields (.field) and methods (.method). baksmali groups them under comments such as # static fields, # instance fields, # direct methods and # virtual methods.

sections.title: A small class with every header directive
Equivalent Java
Access flags
sections.body:
Access flags are written as words before the descriptor. The common class flags are public, final, abstract, interface, annotation, enum and synthetic. An interface is written as abstract interface, because the DEX format stores both flags. An enum class carries the enum flag and extends Ljava/lang/Enum;. A synthetic class was generated by the compiler and has no counterpart in the source, such as a lambda holder.

Class-level private, protected and static do not appear on the .class line: in DEX those flags exist only for nested classes and are recorded in an InnerClass annotation instead.

sections.title: An interface
Inner and anonymous classes
sections.body: Nested classes get their own file and a name joined with $: an inner class Entry of com.acme.demo.Cache is Lcom/acme/demo/Cache$Entry;, and the first anonymous class inside it is Lcom/acme/demo/Cache$1;. A non-static inner class also holds a synthetic field, usually named this$0, that points to the outer instance.

exercises.prompt: Write the header and constructor for a public class com.acme.demo.Task that extends com.acme.demo.BaseTask and implements java.lang.Runnable. The constructor takes no arguments and only calls the superclass constructor. Include a run()V method that does nothing.
exercises.solution:
.class public Lcom/acme/demo/Task;
.super Lcom/acme/demo/BaseTask;
.implements Ljava/lang/Runnable;

.method public constructor <init>()V
    .registers 1
    invoke-direct {p0}, Lcom/acme/demo/BaseTask;-><init>()V
    return-void
.end method

.method public run()V
    .registers 1
    return-void
.end method
exercises.hint: The constructor is named <init>, carries the constructor flag and calls the super constructor with invoke-direct.

exercises.prompt: Declare an enum class com.acme.demo.Level with one static final field LOW of its own type. Only the header and the field are needed.
exercises.hint: Enum classes extend Ljava/lang/Enum; and both the class and its constants carry the enum flag.

quiz.question: How many .super directives can a class have?
options: Two: one for the class and one for its outer class
quiz.explanation: Every class has exactly one direct superclass (java.lang.Object itself is the only exception). Interfaces are listed with separate .implements lines.

quiz.question: What kind of type does this header declare?
options: An abstract class that cannot have methods
quiz.explanation: The interface flag marks an interface; DEX stores it together with abstract, which is why baksmali prints both words.

quiz.question: What is the descriptor of the anonymous class created first inside com.acme.demo.Player?
quiz.explanation: Anonymous classes are numbered in order and joined to the outer name with $, giving Lcom/acme/demo/Player$1;.

quiz.question: What is the .source directive used for?
options: Recording the original source file name for stack traces and debugging
Pointing the assembler at the Java file to compile
Declaring the package of the class
quiz.explanation: .source only stores a file name such as "User.java". It is optional and does not affect how the code behaves; obfuscated builds often remove or rename it.

quiz.question: A class carries the synthetic flag. What does that tell you?
options: The compiler generated it; it has no direct counterpart in the source
It is loaded from native code
It was added by an obfuscator to hide code
quiz.explanation: synthetic marks compiler-generated items, for example lambda classes or accessors. It is a normal part of compiled code, not a sign of tampering.

lessons.title: Methods
lessons.summary: Every piece of executable Smali lives inside a .method block. Learn how a method header is built from access flags, a name and a prototype, how .registers and .locals size the frame, and what makes constructors, static initialisers, abstract and native methods special.

sections.title: Anatomy of a method
sections.body:
A method starts with a .method line and ends with .end method. The header line has three parts:
- access flags such as public, private, static or final,
- the method name,
- the prototype: parameter descriptors in parentheses followed by the return descriptor.

So .method public static max(II)I declares a public static method named max that takes two ints and returns an int. Inside the block come an optional register directive (.registers or .locals), optional metadata such as .param and .annotation, and then the instructions.

sections.title: Four kinds of method in one class
Equivalent Java
.registers versus .locals
sections.body:
.registers N gives the total number of registers in the frame, parameters included. .locals N gives only the registers you use for local values; the assembler adds the parameter registers on top. In the example, getName() uses .locals 1, which is the same as .registers 2: one local (v0) plus one parameter register for this (p0, which is v1).

Both forms produce identical bytecode. baksmali prints .locals by default because it stays correct when you add or remove parameters, while .registers matches the registers_size field stored in the DEX file.

sections.title: Constructors, initialisers and bodiless methods
sections.body:
Constructors are ordinary methods with the reserved name <init>, a void return type and the constructor flag. The first thing a constructor normally does is call a superclass (or another own) <init> with invoke-direct on p0. The static initialiser is named <clinit>, is static, takes no parameters and runs once when the class is initialised; it is where static fields that need code get their values.

Methods marked abstract or native have no body at all: no register directive and no instructions, just the header followed by .end method. Their code is supplied by a subclass or by a native library loaded at runtime.

Some flags only show up in compiled code. A Java synchronized method is marked declared-synchronized, and the compiler inserts explicit monitor-enter and monitor-exit instructions to do the locking. Compilers may also add bridge, synthetic and varargs flags.

sections.title: Do not fall off the end
sections.body: Execution must never run past the last instruction. Every path through a method has to end in a return-*, a throw or a goto back into the code, otherwise the verifier rejects the class. The return instruction must also match the prototype: return-void for V, return-wide for J and D, return-object for references and return for the other primitives.

A constructor that returns without calling a superclass or this-class <init> on p0 leaves the object uninitialised, and the verifier refuses it. When you add a constructor by hand, copy the invoke-direct {p0}, ...-><init> line first.

exercises.prompt: Add a static initialiser to Lcom/acme/demo/Shape; that stores the string "Shape" in the static field TAG of type String.
exercises.starterCode:
.method static constructor <clinit>()V
    .registers 1
    # load the string and store it in Lcom/acme/demo/Shape;->TAG:Ljava/lang/String;
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method static constructor <clinit>()V
    .registers 1
    const-string v0, "Shape"
    sput-object v0, Lcom/acme/demo/Shape;->TAG:Ljava/lang/String;
    return-void
.end method
exercises.hint: Static fields are written with sput-object; the method must still end with return-void.

exercises.prompt: Write a public static method square(I)I that returns its argument multiplied by itself. Use .locals rather than .registers.
exercises.solution:
.method public static square(I)I
    .locals 1
    mul-int v0, p0, p0
    return v0
.end method
exercises.hint: A static method has no this, so its single int parameter is p0.

exercises.prompt: An instance method is declared as .method public update(IJ)V with .registers 6. Rewrite the register directive using .locals.
exercises.solution:
Use .locals 2. The parameters need 4 registers: one for this, one for the int and two for
the long. 6 total registers minus 4 parameter registers leaves 2 locals.
exercises.hint: Count this as one register and every long or double as two.

quiz.question: What does this method header declare?
quiz.code:
.method public static check(Ljava/lang/String;I)Z
    .locals 1
    const/4 v0, 0x1
    return v0
.end method
options: A static method taking a String and an int, returning boolean
An instance method taking a String and an int, returning boolean
A static method taking a boolean, returning a String and an int
A static method taking an int, returning a String
quiz.explanation: The flags say public static, the parentheses list the parameters (Ljava/lang/String; and I), and the descriptor after them is the return type, Z for boolean.

quiz.question: An instance method has one long parameter and uses .locals 3. What is its .registers value?
quiz.explanation: Parameters need 3 registers (1 for this, 2 for the long). 3 locals + 3 parameter registers = 6.

quiz.question: What is the name of a class's static initialiser in Smali?
quiz.explanation: <clinit> is the class initialiser. <init> is the name of every instance constructor.

quiz.question: Which methods are written without .registers/.locals and without instructions?
quiz.explanation: abstract methods are implemented by subclasses and native methods by a native library, so their .method block contains no code.

quiz.question: A method declared to return J ends with return v0. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, return works for every type
It must use return-wide because long is a 64-bit value
It must use return-object because long is boxed
quiz.explanation: long (J) and double (D) are wide values held in a register pair and must be returned with return-wide. The verifier rejects a mismatched return instruction.

lessons.title: Registers
lessons.summary: Dalvik is a register machine: every method works on a fixed array of 32-bit registers instead of an operand stack. Learn the v and p naming schemes, where parameters and this live, how long and double values use register pairs, and why some instructions can only reach v0 to v15.

sections.title: A frame of registers
sections.body:
Each method invocation gets a frame of N registers, where N is the registers_size from the method's code. Registers are numbered v0 to vN-1 and each holds 32 bits: an int, a float, a reference, or half of a 64-bit value. Registers are untyped; the instruction that reads a register decides how its bits are interpreted, and the verifier checks that this is consistent.

The incoming arguments are copied into the last registers of the frame. Smali gives those registers a second name: p0, p1 and so on. If a method has N registers and its parameters need P of them, then pX is simply another name for v(N - P + X).

sections.title: Mapping p registers to v registers
sections.body:
.method public sum(IJ)J
    .registers 6
    # v0-v1: local pair       p0 = v2: this
    # p1 = v3: int a          p2-p3 = v4-v5: long b
    int-to-long v0, p1
    add-long/2addr v0, p2
    return-wide v0
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
this, parameters and wide pairs
sections.body:
For an instance method, p0 always holds this, and the declared parameters start at p1. Static methods have no this, so their first parameter is p0.

long (J) and double (D) values are wide: they occupy two consecutive registers, and you always name the lower one. In the example the long b lives in p2 and p3, and the result of int-to-long fills v0 and v1. Never use the upper half of a pair on its own, and remember that writing to either half destroys the wide value.

To size a frame, count the parameter registers (1 for this, 2 for every J or D, 1 for everything else) and add the locals you need. The sum method needs 4 parameter registers and 2 locals, hence .registers 6, or equivalently .locals 2.

sections.title: How far an instruction can reach
sections.body:
Register numbers are encoded inside the instruction, and many formats only have room for 4 bits:
- 4-bit fields (v0 to v15): formats 11n, 12x, 22c, 22s, 22t and each argument of 35c. That covers const/4, move, the /2addr arithmetic, iget/iput, instance-of, if-eq and the non-range invokes.
- 8-bit fields (v0 to v255): formats such as 11x, 21c, 21s, 22b and 23x, for example const-string, sget, add-int and move-result.
- 16-bit fields (v0 to v65535): move/16, the source of move/from16, and the first register of /range invokes (format 3rc).

Because parameters sit at the top of the frame, a method with many locals can push p0 above v15. The value then has to be copied to a low register (for example with move-object/from16) before a 4-bit instruction can use it.

sections.title: Copying a high register down
sections.body:
.method public static negate(I)I
    .locals 20
    # p0 is v20 here, beyond the 4-bit operands of neg-int (format 12x)
    move/from16 v0, p0
    neg-int v0, v0
    return v0
.end method

sections.title: Editing .locals moves the parameters
sections.body: Increasing .locals in a hand-edited method shifts every p register upwards. Code such as iget v0, p0, ... that assembled before can suddenly fail with a register-out-of-range error. Either keep .locals small or move the parameter into a low register first.

exercises.prompt: A method is declared .method public static compute(JDI)V with .locals 3. Which v register does each p register correspond to?
exercises.solution:
The parameters need 5 registers (2 for J, 2 for D, 1 for I), so the frame has 8 registers.
p0/p1 = v3/v4 hold the long, p2/p3 = v5/v6 hold the double and p4 = v7 holds the int.
exercises.hint: Static methods have no this. Parameters fill the last registers of the frame in order.

exercises.prompt: Write an instance method twice(I)I that returns its argument multiplied by 2, using a single local register.
exercises.solution:
.method public twice(I)I
    .locals 1
    add-int v0, p1, p1
    return v0
.end method
exercises.hint: In an instance method p0 is this, so the int argument is p1.

exercises.prompt: This getter fails to assemble with a register-out-of-range error. Explain why and fix it without reducing .locals.
exercises.starterCode:
.method public getCount()I
    .locals 16
    iget v0, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->count:I
    return v0
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method public getCount()I
    .locals 16
    move-object/from16 v1, p0
    iget v0, v1, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->count:I
    return v0
.end method
exercises.hint: With 16 locals, p0 is v16. iget (format 22c) only has 4-bit register fields.

quiz.question: An instance method (Ljava/lang/String;I)V declares .registers 5. Which register is p0?
quiz.explanation: Parameters need 3 registers (this, String, int), so they occupy v2 to v4 and p0 is v2.

quiz.question: In an instance method, what does p0 contain?
quiz.explanation: Instance methods receive the object they were called on as an implicit first parameter in p0.

quiz.question: How is a long parameter stored?
options: In two consecutive registers, named by the lower one
quiz.explanation: Registers are 32 bits wide, so J and D values take a pair such as p1/p2, referred to as p1.

quiz.question: Why does this method copy p0 into v0 before negating it?
quiz.code:
.method public static negate(I)I
    .locals 20
    move/from16 v0, p0
    neg-int v0, v0
    return v0
.end method
options: p0 is v20, but neg-int (format 12x) only encodes registers v0 to v15
move/from16 converts the int to a long
Parameters are read-only and must be copied before use
quiz.explanation: With .locals 20 and one parameter, p0 maps to v20. Format 12x stores each register in 4 bits, so neg-int v0, p0 would not assemble; move/from16 can read a 16-bit source register.

quiz.question: A static method (JI)V uses .locals 2. What is its total register count?
quiz.explanation: The long needs 2 registers and the int 1, so 3 parameter registers + 2 locals = 5.

lessons.title: Data Types & Descriptors
lessons.summary: Smali writes every type as a compact descriptor: single letters for primitives, L...; for classes and [ for arrays. Learn to read and write descriptors fluently and map them to Java and Kotlin types.

sections.title: Primitive descriptors
sections.body:
Primitive types use one letter each:
- V void (return types only)
- Z boolean
- B byte
- S short
- C char
- I int
- J long
- F float
- D double

The two letters people mix up most are Z (boolean, because B is already byte) and J (long, because L is used for classes).

sections.title: Classes and arrays
sections.body:
A class or interface is written as L, the fully qualified name with slashes instead of dots, and a closing semicolon: java.lang.String becomes Ljava/lang/String;. Nested classes use the $ separator that the compiler puts in the binary name, so java.util.Map.Entry becomes Ljava/util/Map$Entry;.

An array prefixes its element type with one [ per dimension: int[] is [I, String[] is [Ljava/lang/String; and int[][] is [[I. The DEX format allows at most 255 dimensions.

sections.title: Descriptors in field declarations
Equivalent Java
Mapping Kotlin types
sections.body:
Kotlin compiles to the same descriptors. Non-null Int, Long, Boolean and friends become primitives (I, J, Z), while nullable Int? needs an object and becomes Ljava/lang/Integer;. IntArray is [I but Array<Int> is [Ljava/lang/Integer;. Any maps to Ljava/lang/Object;, a Unit return type becomes V, and String is Ljava/lang/String;.

Generic type arguments are erased: List<String> and List<Int> are both Ljava/util/List; in a descriptor. The original generic signature is kept separately in a Signature annotation.

Inside a register, boolean, byte, short and char are all plain 32-bit int values (a boolean is 0 or 1). The descriptor only matters where the type is declared: in field and method references and in typed instructions such as iget-boolean or aget-char.

sections.title: Descriptors are not Java class names
sections.body: Descriptors use slashes, but Class.getName() returns dots ("java.lang.String"), and for arrays a mixed form ("[Ljava.lang.String;"). When you build class names for reflection, do not paste a descriptor in unchanged.

exercises.prompt: Write the descriptors for: char[][], java.lang.Thread.State, Map<String, List<int[]>> and Kotlin's LongArray.
exercises.solution:
char[][] is [[C. java.lang.Thread.State is a nested class, so it is Ljava/lang/Thread$State;.
Generics are erased, so Map<String, List<int[]>> is just Ljava/util/Map;. LongArray is [J.
exercises.hint: Count the brackets, use $ for nested classes and drop everything between < and >.

exercises.prompt: Declare three fields: a public static final long TIMEOUT, a private byte array buffer, and a protected field retries that holds a Kotlin Int?.
exercises.hint: A nullable Int cannot be a primitive, so it is boxed.

quiz.question: What is the descriptor for boolean?
quiz.explanation: boolean is Z. B is byte, and Ljava/lang/Boolean; is the boxed wrapper class.

quiz.question: Which Java type does this field have?
quiz.explanation: Each [ adds one array dimension, so two brackets around Ljava/lang/String; make String[][].

quiz.question: What does the descriptor J stand for?
quiz.explanation: J is long; the letter L was already taken by class descriptors.

quiz.question: A Kotlin property is declared as var retries: Int?. Which descriptor does its field use?
quiz.explanation: A nullable Int must be able to hold null, so Kotlin boxes it as java.lang.Integer.

quiz.question: How is the nested class com.app.Outer.Inner written as a descriptor?
quiz.explanation: Nested classes use their binary name, which joins outer and inner names with $.

lessons.title: Constants
lessons.summary: Dalvik has a family of const instructions that differ only in how many bits of literal they can encode. Learn the exact range of each, how to pick the smallest one, how floats and doubles are loaded as raw bit patterns, and how strings and classes are loaded.

sections.title: The numeric const family
sections.body:
For 32-bit values (int, float, boolean, char, references):
- const/4 vA, #+B: 4-bit signed literal, -8 to 7, and vA must be v0 to v15. One code unit.
- const/16 vAA, #+BBBB: 16-bit signed literal, -32768 to 32767. Two code units.
- const/high16 vAA, #+BBBB0000: sets the top 16 bits and clears the bottom 16. Two code units.
- const vAA, #+BBBBBBBB: any 32-bit value. Three code units.

For 64-bit values (long, double), written to a register pair:
- const-wide/16 vAA, #+BBBB: 16-bit signed, sign-extended to 64 bits.
- const-wide/32 vAA, #+BBBBBBBB: 32-bit signed, sign-extended.
- const-wide/high16 vAA, #+BBBB000000000000: sets only the top 16 bits.
- const-wide vAA, #+BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB: any 64-bit value, five code units.

Compilers always choose the shortest form that can represent the value, and so should you.

sections.title: Picking the smallest encoding
sections.body:
const/4 v0, 0x7
const/4 v1, -0x8
const/16 v2, 0x3e8
const/high16 v3, 0x10000
const v4, 0x186a0
const-wide/16 v5, 0x64
const-wide/32 v7, 0x186a0
const-wide v9, 0x123456789abcL

sections.title: Floats, doubles and null
sections.body:
There are no float-specific const instructions. A float is loaded as its 32-bit IEEE 754 bit pattern and a double as its 64-bit pattern. Many common values have all-zero low bits, which is exactly what the high16 variants are for: 1.0f is 0x3f800000 and 1.0 (double) is 0x3ff0000000000000, so both fit in a high16 instruction. A value like 3.14f (0x4048f5c3) needs the full const.

baksmali prints the decoded value as a comment, which makes these easy to read. The number zero works for every type: const/4 v0, 0x0 is the int 0, the float 0.0f, false, and the null reference.

sections.title: Bit patterns for floating-point values
sections.body:
.method public static defaults()V
    .locals 6
    const/high16 v0, 0x3f800000    # 1.0f
    const v1, 0x4048f5c3           # 3.14f
    const-wide/high16 v2, 0x3ff0000000000000L    # 1.0
    const/4 v4, 0x0                # null, false or 0
    const/4 v5, 0x1                # true
    return-void
.end method

sections.title: Strings and classes
sections.body:
const-string vAA, string@BBBB loads a reference to a string from the DEX string table. The index is 16 bits, so a DEX file with more than 65,536 strings needs const-string/jumbo (a 32-bit index) for the later ones. In Smali you write the literal itself; the assembler picks the index.

const-class vAA, type@BBBB loads the java.lang.Class object for a type, which is what Foo.class compiles to.

sections.title: Loading references
sections.body:
const-string v0, "smali"
const-string/jumbo v1, "used when the string index is above 0xFFFF"
const-class v2, Ljava/lang/String;
const-class v3, [I
Literals are signed. -1 fits in const/4 (const/4 v0, -0x1), but 0xFFFF does not fit in const/16 because it means 65535, not -1. Use const v0, 0xffff for that value.

exercises.prompt: Choose the smallest instruction for each value: 7, -9, 1000, 65536 (0x10000), 100000 and the long 5.
exercises.solution:
7 uses const/4. -9 is outside -8..7, so const/16. 1000 uses const/16. 65536 is 0x00010000,
whose low 16 bits are zero, so const/high16 v0, 0x10000 works. 100000 (0x186a0) needs const.
The long 5 uses const-wide/16.
exercises.hint: Check the signed ranges first, then see whether the low 16 bits are all zero.

exercises.prompt: Write a static method two()F that returns 2.0f using a single const instruction.
exercises.solution:
.method public static two()F
    .locals 1
    const/high16 v0, 0x40000000    # 2.0f
    return v0
.end method
exercises.hint: 2.0f is 0x40000000 in IEEE 754, and floats are returned with the plain return instruction.

exercises.prompt: Load the string "Hello" into v0 and the Class object for java.lang.Integer into v1.
exercises.solution:
const-string v0, "Hello"
const-class v1, Ljava/lang/Integer;
exercises.hint: const-class takes a type descriptor, not a dotted class name.

quiz.question: Which literal range does const/4 support?
quiz.explanation: const/4 (format 11n) stores a signed 4-bit literal, giving -8 to 7.

quiz.question: Which instruction is needed to load 0x7fffffff into v0?
quiz.explanation: The value does not fit in 16 signed bits and its low half is not zero, so only the full 32-bit const can encode it. const-wide/32 would write a register pair.

quiz.question: What float value does v0 hold after this instruction?
options: It is an int, not a float
quiz.explanation: 0x3f800000 is the IEEE 754 single-precision pattern for 1.0. The register just holds bits; it becomes a float when a float instruction or a F-typed return uses it.

quiz.question: When does a compiler use const-string/jumbo instead of const-string?
options: When the string's index in the DEX string table is above 65535
For strings used in more than one class
quiz.explanation: const-string has a 16-bit string index; /jumbo has 32 bits for very large DEX files.

quiz.question: How do you put null into a register?
quiz.explanation: null is the zero reference, so the smallest const with literal 0 loads it.

lessons.title: Method Signatures
lessons.summary: Every call in Smali names its target with a full method reference. Learn the reference syntax, how to read long parameter lists, how overloading, varargs and generics show up, and what the shorty descriptor in the DEX file is.

sections.title: Reading a reference
sections.body:
A method reference has four parts, written without spaces:
- the class that declares or inherits the method, as a descriptor: Ljava/lang/String;
- the arrow ->
- the method name: indexOf
- the prototype: parameter descriptors in parentheses, then the return descriptor: (Ljava/lang/String;I)I

Put together: Ljava/lang/String;->indexOf(Ljava/lang/String;I)I. Field references look similar but use a colon and a single type: Lcom/acme/demo/User;->name:Ljava/lang/String;.

sections.title: Splitting a long parameter list
sections.body:
Long prototypes are just descriptors written back to back. Read them left to right: a primitive is one letter, a class runs up to the next semicolon, and [ attaches to whatever follows it.

(ILjava/lang/String;[JLjava/util/Map;Z)Landroid/os/Bundle; therefore reads as int, String, long[], Map and boolean, returning a Bundle.

sections.title: Varargs are plain arrays
Equivalent Java
Overloads, varargs and bridges
sections.body:
The one-line Java call hides two conversions that Smali makes visible. The int is boxed with Integer.valueOf because the varargs parameter is Object..., and the arguments are packed into a new Object[] because a varargs parameter is an ordinary array in the descriptor. The varargs access flag on the declaration is only a hint for compilers.

Overloads are distinct references: append(I) and append(Ljava/lang/String;) are different methods. The return type is part of the reference too, so the bytecode can contain two methods that differ only in return type. Java source cannot, but javac creates exactly that when it adds a synthetic bridge method for a covariant override.

sections.title: Generics survive only in a Signature annotation
sections.body:
.method public setNames(Ljava/util/List;)V
    .locals 0
    .annotation system Ldalvik/annotation/Signature;
        value = {
            "(",
            "Ljava/util/List<",
            "Ljava/lang/String;",
            ">;)V"
        }
    .end annotation
    return-void
.end method

Each prototype in the DEX file also stores a shorty descriptor: the return type followed by the parameters, with every class or array type collapsed to L. (ILjava/lang/String;[J)Z has the shorty ZILL. You will meet shorties in DEX dumps and in native (JNI) tooling.

sections.title: Signatures are matched exactly
sections.body: The assembler does not check that a referenced method exists. A typo in a name or a wrong return type assembles fine and only fails when the call is resolved at runtime, typically with NoSuchMethodError.

exercises.prompt: Write the method reference for SharedPreferences.getBoolean(String key, boolean defValue), declared in the interface android.content.SharedPreferences.
exercises.solution: Landroid/content/SharedPreferences;->getBoolean(Ljava/lang/String;Z)Z
exercises.hint: Interfaces use the same reference syntax as classes. boolean is Z.

exercises.prompt: Two longs are stored in the register pairs v0/v1 and v2/v3. Call Math.max(long, long) and put the result back in v0/v1.
exercises.solution:
invoke-static {v0, v1, v2, v3}, Ljava/lang/Math;->max(JJ)J
move-result-wide v0
exercises.hint: Non-range invokes list both registers of each wide argument, and a J result needs move-result-wide.

exercises.prompt:
Translate this prototype into Java parameter and return types:
(Landroid/content/Context;[[ILjava/lang/CharSequence;J)[Ljava/lang/String;
exercises.solution: Parameters: Context, int[][], CharSequence and long. Return type: String[].
exercises.hint: Split at each semicolon and remember that [[ belongs to the I after it.

quiz.question: What does this reference describe?
options: A field named indexOf of type int
quiz.explanation: The parentheses hold Ljava/lang/String; and I, and the final I is the int return type.

quiz.question: How does a Java varargs parameter String... args appear in a prototype?
quiz.explanation: Varargs compile to an ordinary array parameter; only the varargs access flag marks the method.

quiz.question: What does List<String> become in a method descriptor?
quiz.explanation: Type arguments are erased from descriptors. The generic form is only kept in the dalvik.annotation.Signature annotation.

quiz.question: What is the shorty descriptor of the prototype (J[ILjava/lang/Object;)V?
quiz.explanation: The shorty starts with the return type (V), then lists parameters with every reference or array type as L.

quiz.question: A hand-written invoke uses the wrong return type in its method reference. What happens?
options: smali refuses to assemble the file
The return value is converted automatically
It assembles, but the call fails at runtime with NoSuchMethodError
The method is called and the result is discarded
quiz.explanation: The assembler only checks syntax. Method resolution happens at runtime and matches the name and the full prototype, including the return type.

lessons.title: Method Invocation
lessons.summary: Learn the five invoke instructions, how the runtime chooses the method each one calls, when the /range forms are needed, and how return values are collected with move-result, move-result-wide and move-result-object.

sections.title: Five ways to call a method
sections.body:
Every method call in Dalvik bytecode is one of five invoke kinds. They differ in how the target method is found at run time:
- invoke-virtual: a normal instance method that may be overridden. The runtime looks at the actual class of the receiver object and dispatches to the most specific override.
- invoke-super: the closest superclass implementation of a virtual method, skipping any override in the calling class. This is how super.method() is compiled.
- invoke-direct: an instance method that cannot be overridden, namely a private method or a constructor (<init>). No dynamic lookup is needed.
- invoke-static: a static method. There is no receiver object.
- invoke-interface: a method called through an interface type, such as List or Runnable.

The first register in the braces is the receiver (this) for every kind except invoke-static; the remaining registers are the arguments in declaration order.

sections.title: All five invoke kinds
sections.body:
.class public Lcom/acme/demo/Player;
.super Lcom/acme/demo/Entity;

.field private listener:Ljava/lang/Runnable;

.method public constructor <init>()V
    .registers 1
    # a superclass constructor is always called with invoke-direct
    invoke-direct {p0}, Lcom/acme/demo/Entity;-><init>()V
    return-void
.end method

.method private heal(I)V
    .registers 2
    return-void
.end method

.method public update()V
    .registers 5

    # virtual: dispatched on the runtime class of p0
    invoke-virtual {p0}, Lcom/acme/demo/Player;->getName()Ljava/lang/String;
    move-result-object v0

    # super: the parent's implementation, never an override
    invoke-super {p0}, Lcom/acme/demo/Entity;->update()V

    # direct: a private method of this class
    const/16 v1, 0xa
    invoke-direct {p0, v1}, Lcom/acme/demo/Player;->heal(I)V

    # static: no receiver register
    invoke-static {v0}, Landroid/text/TextUtils;->isEmpty(Ljava/lang/CharSequence;)Z
    move-result v2

    # interface: the declared type is an interface
    iget-object v3, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Player;->listener:Ljava/lang/Runnable;
    invoke-interface {v3}, Ljava/lang/Runnable;->run()V

    return-void
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
Getting the result back
sections.body:
An invoke never writes a register. The return value goes into a hidden result slot, and the very next instruction must copy it out if you want to keep it:
- move-result vAA for int, boolean, byte, char, short and float results,
- move-result-wide vAA for long and double results (it writes the pair vAA and vAA+1),
- move-result-object vAA for references, including arrays.

If you do not need the value, simply omit the move-result. Placing any other instruction between the invoke and its move-result makes the method invalid, and the verifier rejects the class.

sections.title: Wide results and wide arguments
sections.body:
.method public static elapsedSince(J)Ljava/lang/Long;
    .registers 5

    invoke-static {}, Ljava/lang/System;->currentTimeMillis()J
    move-result-wide v0

    sub-long/2addr v0, p0

    # a long argument occupies two registers in the list
    invoke-static {v0, v1}, Ljava/lang/Long;->valueOf(J)Ljava/lang/Long;
    move-result-object v2
    return-object v2
.end method

sections.title: The five-register limit and /range
sections.body:
The regular invoke instructions use format 35c: they can list at most five argument registers, each a 4-bit register number (v0-v15). The receiver counts as one of the five, and every long or double argument counts as two because it lives in a register pair.

When a call needs more than five argument words, or the arguments live in registers above v15, the compiler uses the /range variant (format 3rc). It takes a contiguous block written as {vN .. vM}, so the arguments must first be placed in consecutive registers, in order.

sections.title: Six arguments need invoke-static/range
sections.body:
.method public static sum6(IIIIII)I
    .registers 6
    add-int/2addr p0, p1
    add-int/2addr p0, p2
    add-int/2addr p0, p3
    add-int/2addr p0, p4
    add-int/2addr p0, p5
    return p0
.end method

.method public static demo()I
    .registers 6
    const/4 v0, 0x1
    const/4 v1, 0x2
    const/4 v2, 0x3
    const/4 v3, 0x4
    const/4 v4, 0x5
    const/4 v5, 0x6
    invoke-static/range {v0 .. v5}, Lcom/acme/demo/MathUtil;->sum6(IIIIII)I
    move-result v0
    return v0
.end method

To pick the invoke kind when writing Smali by hand, ask two questions: is there a receiver (if not, invoke-static), and can the call be overridden? Private methods and constructors use invoke-direct, super calls use invoke-super, calls through an interface type use invoke-interface, and everything else is invoke-virtual.

exercises.prompt: Complete the static method len(Ljava/lang/String;)I so it returns the length of its argument by calling String.length().
exercises.starterCode:
.method public static len(Ljava/lang/String;)I
    .registers 2
    # call length() on p0 and return the result
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method public static len(Ljava/lang/String;)I
    .registers 2
    invoke-virtual {p0}, Ljava/lang/String;->length()I
    move-result v0
    return v0
.end method
exercises.hint: String is a class, not an interface, and length() returns an int: invoke-virtual then move-result.

exercises.prompt: This call passes six int arguments and does not assemble. Rewrite it so it works, keeping the arguments in v0-v5.
exercises.starterCode:
invoke-static {v0, v1, v2, v3, v4, v5}, Lcom/acme/demo/MathUtil;->sum6(IIIIII)I
move-result v0
exercises.solution:
invoke-static/range {v0 .. v5}, Lcom/acme/demo/MathUtil;->sum6(IIIIII)I
move-result v0
exercises.hint: The 35c format holds at most five registers. The 3rc format takes a contiguous range instead.

exercises.prompt: Name the invoke instruction for each call: (a) list.size() where list is declared as java.util.List, (b) a call to a private helper method, (c) Math.max(a, b), (d) super.onCreate() inside an Activity subclass.
exercises.solution:
(a) invoke-interface, because List is an interface. (b) invoke-direct, because private methods
cannot be overridden. (c) invoke-static, because Math.max is static. (d) invoke-super, which calls
the superclass implementation directly.
exercises.hint: Look at the declared type of the receiver and the method's modifiers, not at the object's runtime class.

quiz.question: Which instruction is used to call a private instance method of the same class?
quiz.explanation: Private instance methods and constructors are not overridable, so they are called with invoke-direct. invoke-static is only for methods without a receiver.

quiz.question: In this call, which registers hold the long argument?
quiz.explanation: v0 is the receiver (this). A long occupies a register pair, so it is passed in v1 and v2, and both registers appear in the argument list.

quiz.question: A call needs seven argument words. What must the compiler emit?
options: An invoke-*/range instruction with the arguments in consecutive registers
An invoke with seven registers in braces
A filled-new-array to pack the arguments
quiz.explanation: Format 35c lists at most five registers. The /range forms (format 3rc) take a contiguous block of registers, {vN .. vM}, so more arguments can be passed.

quiz.question: What happens with this code?
quiz.code:
invoke-virtual {v0}, Ljava/lang/String;->length()I
const/4 v2, 0x0
move-result v1
options: v1 receives the length after the const
The result is kept until the next invoke
quiz.explanation: move-result must be the instruction immediately after the invoke. Any instruction in between makes the method invalid, which is reported as a verification error when the class loads.

quiz.question: What does invoke-super do differently from invoke-virtual?
options: It calls the closest superclass implementation instead of dispatching to an override
It calls the method on the superclass object instead of this
It calls static methods of the superclass
It is only used for constructors
quiz.explanation: invoke-super still passes this as the receiver, but it skips dynamic dispatch and runs the nearest superclass implementation. Superclass constructors use invoke-direct instead.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.summary: Create, read and write arrays in Smali: new-array and array-length, the typed aget/aput family, filled-new-array for small literal arrays, fill-array-data payloads, and the exceptions array instructions can throw.

sections.title: Creating and indexing arrays
sections.body:
Arrays are objects, so a register holds only a reference to one. new-array vA, vB, [T creates an array of type [T whose length is the int in vB, and stores the reference in vA. All elements start as zero, false or null. array-length vA, vB stores the length of the array in vB into vA.

Elements are read with aget and written with aput. Both take three registers: the value, the array and the int index. The suffix must match the element type:
- aget / aput: int and float elements (any 32-bit primitive that is not one of the types below),
- aget-wide / aput-wide: long and double, using a register pair for the value,
- aget-object / aput-object: references, including nested arrays,
- aget-boolean, aget-byte, aget-char, aget-short and the matching aput variants.

sections.title: Writing and reading elements
sections.body:
.method public static names()[Ljava/lang/String;
    .registers 3
    const/4 v0, 0x2
    new-array v0, v0, [Ljava/lang/String;

    const/4 v1, 0x0
    const-string v2, "alpha"
    aput-object v2, v0, v1

    const/4 v1, 0x1
    const-string v2, "beta"
    aput-object v2, v0, v1

    return-object v0
.end method

.method public static sum([I)I
    .registers 5
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    const/4 v1, 0x0
    array-length v2, p0
    :loop
    if-ge v1, v2, :done
    aget v3, p0, v1
    add-int/2addr v0, v3
    add-int/lit8 v1, v1, 0x1
    goto :loop
    :done
    return v0
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
Literal arrays
sections.body:
Two instructions build arrays from literal values more compactly.

filled-new-array {vC, ...}, [T creates an array whose length is the number of registers listed and fills it with their values. The elements must be single-word values, so it cannot build long[] or double[] arrays, but int and reference arrays are fine. Like an invoke, it does not write a register itself: a move-result-object must follow immediately. filled-new-array/range accepts a contiguous range of registers for longer lists.

fill-array-data vAA, :label copies constant data into an existing primitive array. The label points to an .array-data block (the fill-array-data-payload pseudo-instruction) whose number is the element width in bytes: 1 for byte and boolean, 2 for char and short, 4 for int and float, 8 for long and double. The payload is data, not code, so it is placed where execution can never fall into it, typically after the method's final return.

sections.title: fill-array-data and filled-new-array
sections.body:
.method public static primes()[I
    .registers 1
    const/4 v0, 0x5
    new-array v0, v0, [I
    fill-array-data v0, :array_0
    return-object v0

    :array_0
    .array-data 4
        0x2
        0x3
        0x5
        0x7
        0xb
    .end array-data
.end method

.method public static triple()[I
    .registers 4
    const/4 v0, 0x1
    const/4 v1, 0x2
    const/4 v2, 0x3
    filled-new-array {v0, v1, v2}, [I
    move-result-object v3
    return-object v3
.end method

sections.title: Run-time checks
sections.body: Array instructions check their operands at run time. A null array reference throws NullPointerException, an index below zero or at least the length throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, new-array with a negative size throws NegativeArraySizeException, and aput-object throws ArrayStoreException when the value's type is not assignable to the array's element type (for example an Integer stored into a String[] seen through an Object[] reference).

There is no separate aget-float: float arrays use plain aget and aput, just like int arrays. The instruction only cares about the element width, while the array type decides how the bits are interpreted.

exercises.prompt: Write first([Ljava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String; that returns element 0 of its argument.
exercises.solution:
.method public static first([Ljava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String;
    .registers 2
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    aget-object v0, p0, v0
    return-object v0
.end method
exercises.hint: Put the index 0 in a register first, then use the -object variant because the elements are references.

exercises.prompt: Write make()[J that creates a long[] of length 2, stores 10L at index 1 and returns it.
exercises.solution:
.method public static make()[J
    .registers 4
    const/4 v0, 0x2
    new-array v0, v0, [J
    const/4 v1, 0x1
    const-wide/16 v2, 0xa
    aput-wide v2, v0, v1
    return-object v0
.end method
exercises.hint: A long value needs a register pair (here v2 and v3) and the -wide variant of aput.

quiz.question: Which instruction reads an element from a char[] array?
quiz.explanation: char elements are 16-bit unsigned values and use aget-char. aget-short would sign-extend the value, which gives wrong results for characters above 0x7fff.

quiz.question: Which instruction reads an element from a float[] array?
quiz.explanation: There is no aget-float. Plain aget handles all 32-bit non-reference elements other than the narrow types, which includes both int and float.

quiz.question: In this payload, what does the 4 after .array-data mean?
quiz.explanation: The number is the width of each element: 4 bytes for int or float. The element count is implied by the number of values listed before .end array-data.

quiz.question: Storing an Integer into a String[] through an Object[] reference with aput-object throws what?
quiz.explanation: aput-object checks that the value is assignable to the array's actual element type at run time and throws ArrayStoreException if it is not.

quiz.question: What must follow filled-new-array if the new array is going to be used?
quiz.explanation: filled-new-array stores its result like an invoke does, so the array reference has to be copied with move-result-object as the very next instruction.

lessons.title: Conditions
lessons.summary: Branch with if-test and if-testz instructions and labels, recognise the inverted conditions compilers generate, test references for null, and compare long, float and double values with cmp-long and the NaN-aware cmpl/cmpg instructions.

sections.title: Two families of branches
sections.body:
Dalvik has two families of conditional branches. The if-test family compares two registers:
if-eq, if-ne, if-lt, if-ge, if-gt and if-le. The if-testz family compares one register against zero: if-eqz, if-nez, if-ltz, if-gez, if-gtz and if-lez. When the condition holds, execution jumps to the label; otherwise it continues with the next instruction.

Labels are names that start with a colon, such as :cond_0. baksmali generates names like :cond_0 and :goto_0, but any name works when you write Smali by hand. In the binary, the label becomes a signed offset measured in 16-bit code units.

sections.title: Inverted condition
sections.body:
.method public static max(II)I
    .registers 2
    if-le p0, p1, :cond_0
    return p0

    :cond_0
    return p1
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
Reading compiled conditions
sections.body:
Notice that the Java condition is a > b, yet the Smali tests a <= b. Compilers usually emit the opposite condition and jump over the then-block, so the then-block can follow the branch directly. When you translate Smali back to Java in your head, invert the test first.

The if-testz instructions cover several Java idioms. Booleans are stored as 0 or 1, so if (flag) becomes if-eqz flag, :else. A reference compared with zero is a null check: if-eqz jumps when the reference is null and if-nez when it is not. if-eq and if-ne on two references compare identity, exactly like == in Java; calling equals() needs a real invoke.

sections.title: Null checks and long comparisons
sections.body:
.method public static lengthOrZero(Ljava/lang/String;)I
    .registers 2
    if-nez p0, :cond_0
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    return v0

    :cond_0
    invoke-virtual {p0}, Ljava/lang/String;->length()I
    move-result v0
    return v0
.end method

.method public static isBefore(JJ)Z
    .registers 5
    cmp-long v0, p0, p2
    if-gez v0, :cond_0
    const/4 v0, 0x1
    return v0

    :cond_0
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    return v0
.end method

sections.title: Comparing long, float and double
sections.body:
The if instructions only work on int-like values and references. For long, float and double, a compare instruction first produces -1, 0 or 1 in an int register, and an if-testz branches on that result. cmp-long compares two long pairs.

Floating-point values can be NaN, which is not less than, equal to or greater than anything. The two compare variants differ only in what they return for NaN: cmpl-float and cmpl-double ("lt bias") return -1, while cmpg-float and cmpg-double ("gt bias") return 1. A compiler picks the variant that makes the comparison false when NaN is involved: cmpg for < and <=, cmpl for > and >=.

sections.title: A NaN-safe float test
sections.body:
.method public static isPositive(F)Z
    .registers 3
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    # NaN gives -1 here, so the method returns false for NaN
    cmpl-float v1, p0, v0
    if-lez v1, :cond_0
    const/4 v0, 0x1

    :cond_0
    return v0
.end method

Branch offsets are 16-bit for all if instructions, so a conditional jump reaches about 32K code units in each direction. if-test registers are 4-bit (v0-v15) because format 22t packs two registers into one byte, while if-testz uses format 21t with an 8-bit register (v0-v255).

exercises.prompt: Write isZero(I)Z that returns true when its argument is 0 and false otherwise.
exercises.solution:
.method public static isZero(I)Z
    .registers 2
    if-nez p0, :not_zero
    const/4 v0, 0x1
    return v0

    :not_zero
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    return v0
.end method
exercises.hint: Jump away when the value is not zero; booleans are returned as the ints 1 and 0.

exercises.prompt: Write min(II)I equivalent to the Java expression a < b ? a : b, using a single if-test instruction.
exercises.solution:
.method public static min(II)I
    .registers 2
    if-ge p0, p1, :cond_0
    return p0

    :cond_0
    return p1
.end method
exercises.hint: Invert the condition: jump to the code that returns b when a >= b.

exercises.prompt: Which compare instruction and which branch would a compiler typically use for the Java test if (d < 1.0) { ... } where d is a double held in a register pair?
exercises.solution:
cmpg-double, because the condition uses <: a NaN operand makes cmpg return 1, so the test is false.
The result is then branched on with if-gez, which skips the then-block when the result is 0 or 1.
exercises.hint: Choose the bias that turns NaN into the 'false' answer, then invert the branch.

quiz.question: When does this instruction jump to :cond_0?
quiz.explanation: if-gtz branches when the register is greater than zero.

quiz.question: This Smali was compiled from an if statement, with a in v0 and b in v1. Which Java condition guards the return v0?
quiz.code:
if-le v0, v1, :cond_0
return v0
:cond_0
return v1
quiz.explanation: The branch jumps past return v0 when a <= b, so return v0 runs only when a > b. Compilers emit the inverted condition to skip over the then-block.

quiz.question: How is a comparison of two long values usually compiled?
options: cmp-long into an int register, followed by an if-testz
sub-long followed by if-ltz on the high half
quiz.explanation: The if instructions work only on single-word values. cmp-long writes -1, 0 or 1 to an int register, and an if-testz branches on it.

quiz.question: What does cmpl-float return when one operand is NaN?
quiz.explanation: cmpl has an "lt bias" and returns -1 for NaN comparisons; cmpg returns 1. No exception is thrown.

quiz.question: What does if-eq v0, v1 test when both registers hold String references?
options: Whether the strings have the same characters
Whether both references point to the same object
Whether the strings have the same length
quiz.explanation: if-eq on references compares identity, like == in Java. Comparing contents requires calling equals() with an invoke instruction.

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.summary: Recognise for, while and do-while loops in Smali by their backward branches, walk arrays with array-length and aget, follow the iterator calls behind an enhanced for loop, and see how break and continue become plain jumps.

sections.title: Loops are backward jumps
sections.body:
Dalvik has no loop instruction. A loop is simply a branch that jumps backwards to an earlier label, called a back-edge. Once you spot a goto or if instruction whose target is above it, you have found a loop; the label it jumps to is the loop head.

A typical for or while loop compiled by d8 looks like this: the condition is tested at the top with an inverted if that exits the loop, the body follows, then the update step, and finally a goto jumps back to the condition. A do-while loop puts the test at the bottom instead, so the back-edge is the conditional branch itself.

sections.title: A for loop and a do-while loop
sections.body:
.method public static sumTo(I)I
    .registers 3
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    const/4 v1, 0x1

    :goto_0
    if-gt v1, p0, :cond_0
    add-int/2addr v0, v1
    add-int/lit8 v1, v1, 0x1
    goto :goto_0

    :cond_0
    return v0
.end method

.method public static countDigits(I)I
    .registers 3
    const/4 v0, 0x0

    :loop
    add-int/lit8 v0, v0, 0x1
    div-int/lit8 p0, p0, 0xa
    if-nez p0, :loop

    return v0
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
Iterator loops
sections.body:
An enhanced for loop over an Iterable has no special bytecode. The compiler calls iterator() once, then repeatedly calls hasNext() and next() through invoke-interface. Because of generic type erasure, next() returns Object, so a check-cast to the element type follows it.

Loops over arrays usually load array-length into a register before the loop and compare the index against it with if-ge.

sections.title: for (String s : list) System.out.println(s);
sections.body:
.method public static printAll(Ljava/util/List;)V
    .registers 4
    invoke-interface {p0}, Ljava/util/List;->iterator()Ljava/util/Iterator;
    move-result-object v0

    :goto_0
    invoke-interface {v0}, Ljava/util/Iterator;->hasNext()Z
    move-result v1
    if-eqz v1, :cond_0

    invoke-interface {v0}, Ljava/util/Iterator;->next()Ljava/lang/Object;
    move-result-object v1
    check-cast v1, Ljava/lang/String;

    sget-object v2, Ljava/lang/System;->out:Ljava/io/PrintStream;
    invoke-virtual {v2, v1}, Ljava/io/PrintStream;->println(Ljava/lang/String;)V
    goto :goto_0

    :cond_0
    return-void
.end method

sections.title: break and continue
sections.body: break and continue compile to ordinary jumps. break jumps to the first instruction after the loop, and continue jumps to the update step (in a for loop) or the condition (in a while loop). In the listing below, a zero element ends the loop early and negative elements are skipped.

sections.title: break and continue as jumps
sections.body:
.method public static sumUntilZero([I)I
    .registers 5
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    const/4 v1, 0x0
    array-length v2, p0

    :loop
    if-ge v1, v2, :end
    aget v3, p0, v1
    # break
    if-eqz v3, :end
    # continue
    if-ltz v3, :next
    add-int/2addr v0, v3

    :next
    add-int/lit8 v1, v1, 0x1
    goto :loop

    :end
    return v0
.end method

When reading an unfamiliar loop, find three things: the loop head (target of the back-edge), the exit branch (the if that jumps past the back-edge) and the induction variable (usually updated with add-int/lit8 just before the goto).

exercises.prompt: Write an iterative factorial(I)I that multiplies the result by n and decrements n until n is no longer positive.
exercises.starterCode:
.method public static factorial(I)I
    .registers 2
    const/4 v0, 0x1
    # loop while p0 > 0
    return v0
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method public static factorial(I)I
    .registers 2
    const/4 v0, 0x1

    :loop
    if-lez p0, :done
    mul-int/2addr v0, p0
    add-int/lit8 p0, p0, -0x1
    goto :loop

    :done
    return v0
.end method
exercises.hint: Test the exit condition at the loop head with if-lez, and close the loop with goto.

exercises.prompt: Write countTrue([Z)I that returns how many elements of a boolean[] are true.
exercises.solution:
.method public static countTrue([Z)I
    .registers 5
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    const/4 v1, 0x0
    array-length v2, p0

    :loop
    if-ge v1, v2, :done
    aget-boolean v3, p0, v1
    if-eqz v3, :next
    add-int/lit8 v0, v0, 0x1

    :next
    add-int/lit8 v1, v1, 0x1
    goto :loop

    :done
    return v0
.end method
exercises.hint: Use aget-boolean for the element and skip the increment with if-eqz when it is false.

quiz.question: What identifies a loop in Smali?
options: A branch whose target label comes before the branch
