quiz.explanation: There is no loop instruction or directive. A loop exists wherever a goto or if jumps back to an earlier instruction. Label names are arbitrary.

quiz.question: Which Java loop does this Smali correspond to?
quiz.code:
:loop
add-int/lit8 v0, v0, 0x1
div-int/lit8 p0, p0, 0xa
if-nez p0, :loop
quiz.explanation: The body runs before the condition is checked, and the back-edge is the conditional branch at the bottom. That is the shape of a do-while loop.

quiz.question: How is for (String s : list) compiled when list is a java.util.List?
options: With iterator(), hasNext() and next() called through invoke-interface
quiz.explanation: An enhanced for loop over an Iterable uses the Iterator protocol. The calls go through invoke-interface because List and Iterator are interfaces.

quiz.question: In a compiled for loop, where does continue usually jump?
options: To the update step before the back-edge
To the first instruction of the method
To the end of the loop
quiz.explanation: continue skips the rest of the body but still runs the update (for example i++), so it jumps to the update step, which then goes back to the condition.

quiz.question: Why does a check-cast follow Iterator.next() in a loop over List<String>?
options: next() returns Object because of generic type erasure
To convert the value to a primitive
quiz.explanation: Generic type parameters are erased, so the method reference returns Ljava/lang/Object;. The check-cast restores the static type and throws ClassCastException on a wrong element.

lessons.title: Fields
lessons.summary: Declare static and instance fields with .field, read and write them with the iget/iput and sget/sput families, understand the field reference syntax, and see where static initialisers and constants end up in the compiled class.

sections.title: Declaring and referencing fields
sections.body:
A field is declared with .field followed by its access flags, its name and its type descriptor, for example .field private count:I. Static fields add the static flag.

Instructions refer to a field with a full field reference: the defining class, an arrow, the name, a colon and the type, as in Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->count:I. The type is part of the reference, so the same name with a different type would be a different field.

sections.title: Static and instance fields
sections.body:
.class public Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;
.super Ljava/lang/Object;

.field public static final MAX:I = 0x64
.field private static instances:I

.field private count:I
.field private name:Ljava/lang/String;
.field private total:J

.method public constructor <init>(Ljava/lang/String;)V
    .registers 3
    invoke-direct {p0}, Ljava/lang/Object;-><init>()V
    iput-object p1, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->name:Ljava/lang/String;

    sget v0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->instances:I
    add-int/lit8 v0, v0, 0x1
    sput v0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->instances:I
    return-void
.end method

.method public increment()V
    .registers 6
    iget v0, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->count:I
    add-int/lit8 v0, v0, 0x1
    iput v0, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->count:I

    iget-wide v1, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->total:J
    const-wide/16 v3, 0x1
    add-long/2addr v1, v3
    iput-wide v1, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->total:J
    return-void
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
The get and put families
sections.body:
Instance fields use iget and iput with three operands: the value register, the object register and the field reference. Static fields use sget and sput, which have no object register. Both families have typed variants that must match the field's type:
- iget / iput and sget / sput: int and float,
- -wide: long and double, using a register pair,
- -object: any reference type, including arrays,
- -boolean, -byte, -char and -short for the narrow types.

iget and iput use format 22c, so their two registers must be v0-v15. sget and sput use format 21c with a single 8-bit register.

sections.title: Static initialisation in <clinit>
Initial values and <clinit>
sections.body:
A static field can carry an initial value directly in its .field line, like MAX:I = 0x64 above. The value is stored in the class definition and assigned when the class is initialised. Compilers use this for compile-time constants (primitives and strings). Java compilers also inline such constants at every use site, so other classes often contain const/16 v0, 0x64 instead of an sget.

Every other static initialiser, such as creating the ArrayList, becomes code in the static constructor <clinit>, which runs once before the class is first used. Instance field initialisers cannot be expressed in the .field line at all: they become iput instructions inside each constructor.

The instruction must match the field: using iget on a static field, or sget on an instance field, throws IncompatibleClassChangeError, and a reference to a field that does not exist throws NoSuchFieldError. A mismatched type variant, such as iget on a long field, fails verification.

exercises.prompt: Write the getter getName()Ljava/lang/String; for the Counter class above.
exercises.hint: The receiver is p0, the field holds a reference, so use the -object variant of iget.

exercises.prompt: Declare a private static boolean field enabled in Lcom/acme/demo/Settings; and write a static method enable()V that sets it to true.
exercises.solution:
.field private static enabled:Z

.method public static enable()V
    .registers 1
    const/4 v0, 0x1
    sput-boolean v0, Lcom/acme/demo/Settings;->enabled:Z
    return-void
.end method
exercises.hint: Booleans are written as 0 or 1 with sput-boolean; static writes need no object register.

quiz.question: In this field reference, what does the final I mean?
options: The field is an instance field
quiz.explanation: The part after the colon is the field's type descriptor, and I is the descriptor for int.

quiz.question: Which instruction reads an instance field of type double?
quiz.explanation: long and double fields are 64-bit and use the -wide variants. Instance fields use iget, static fields sget.

quiz.question: What does this instruction do?
options: Reads the static field System.out into v0
Reads the instance field out of the object in v0
quiz.explanation: sget-object reads a static reference field. The value of System.out, a PrintStream, is stored in v0. There is no object operand because the field is static.

quiz.question: Where do Java instance field initialisers such as private int count = 5; end up?
options: As iput instructions in the constructors
In a separate initialiser method called <finit>
quiz.explanation: Initial values in the .field line are only supported for static fields. Instance initialisers are compiled into each constructor, after the superclass constructor call.

quiz.question: Why might another class read Counter.MAX with const/16 instead of sget?
options: The Java compiler inlined the compile-time constant
d8 converts every static field into a constant
MAX is stored in a register
quiz.explanation: Compile-time constants (static final primitives and strings with constant initialisers) are copied into the code of the classes that use them, so no field access remains.

lessons.title: Arithmetic
lessons.summary: Dalvik has a separate instruction for every arithmetic operation and operand type. Learn the three-register, /2addr and literal forms, reverse subtraction, masked shifts, division by zero, 64-bit register pairs and the conversion instructions.

sections.title: One opcode per operation and type
sections.body:
Arithmetic instructions are typed: add-int adds two 32-bit ints, add-long two 64-bit longs, add-float and add-double floating-point values. The register itself carries no type; the opcode decides how its bits are interpreted, and the verifier checks that the types line up.

Each binary operation exists in up to four shapes:
- binop vAA, vBB, vCC (format 23x): three 8-bit registers, so any of v0..v255.
- binop/2addr vA, vB (format 12x): vA is both the first source and the destination. Both registers are 4-bit, so only v0..v15, but the instruction is a single 16-bit code unit.
- binop/lit16 vA, vB, #+CCCC (format 22s): 4-bit registers and a signed 16-bit constant.
- binop/lit8 vAA, vBB, #+CC (format 22b): 8-bit registers and a signed 8-bit constant.

Literal forms exist only for int operations. /lit16 covers add, rsub, mul, div, rem, and, or and xor; /lit8 adds the three shifts on top of those.

Because /2addr, /lit16 and the unary operations use 4-bit register fields, they only work when every register involved is v0..v15. In large methods the parameter registers can sit above v15, so compilers copy values down with move/from16 or use the 23x and 22b forms instead.

sections.title: Three shapes in one method
sections.body:
.method public static compute(II)I
    .registers 4
    # p0 = a, p1 = b
    add-int v0, p0, p1          # v0 = a + b
    mul-int/lit8 v0, v0, 0xa    # v0 = v0 * 10
    div-int v1, p0, p1          # v1 = a / b  (throws if b == 0)
    sub-int/2addr v0, v1        # v0 = v0 - v1
    return v0
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
Constants, reverse subtraction and shifts
sections.body:
There is no sub-int/lit8 or sub-int/lit16. To subtract a constant, compilers add its negative:
x - 5 becomes add-int/lit8 v0, v0, -0x5. The opposite case, constant minus register, uses the reverse-subtract instructions: rsub-int vA, vB, #+CCCC (the /lit16 member of the family, written without a suffix) and rsub-int/lit8 vAA, vBB, #+CC both compute literal - vB.

Shifts mask their distance: shl-int, shr-int and ushr-int use only the low 5 bits of the shift amount (b & 0x1f), the long variants only the low 6 bits. Shifting an int by 33 therefore shifts by 1, exactly as in Java. shr is the arithmetic (sign-preserving) shift, ushr the logical one.

sections.title: Literal forms in practice
sections.body:
.method public static literals(I)V
    .registers 8
    # p0 = x (also known as v7)
    rsub-int/lit8 v0, p0, 0x64      # v0 = 100 - x
    rsub-int v1, p0, 0x3e8          # v1 = 1000 - x (16-bit literal form)
    add-int/lit8 v2, p0, -0x1       # v2 = x - 1
    shl-int/lit8 v3, p0, 0x3        # v3 = x << 3
    ushr-int/lit8 v4, p0, 0x1f      # v4 = sign bit of x (0 or 1)
    neg-int v5, p0                  # v5 = -x
    not-int v6, p0                  # v6 = ~x (ones' complement)
    return-void
.end method

sections.title: Wide values and conversions
sections.body:
Longs and doubles occupy register pairs. In add-long v0, v2, v4 the result goes to v0 and v1, and the operands are read from v2/v3 and v4/v5; you only ever write the lower register number. The exception is the shift distance of shl-long, shr-long and ushr-long, which is a single int register.

Conversions are unary instructions in format 12x: int-to-long, long-to-int (keeps the low 32 bits), int-to-float, float-to-int, double-to-long and so on. float-to-int and double-to-int round toward zero, turn NaN into 0 and clamp out-of-range values to the int minimum or maximum. int-to-byte and int-to-short truncate with sign extension; int-to-char truncates to 16 bits without sign extension.

sections.title: Working with register pairs
sections.body:
.method public static average(JJ)J
    .registers 8
    # p0/p1 = a, p2/p3 = b (each long uses two registers)
    add-long v0, p0, p2             # v0/v1 = a + b
    const-wide/16 v2, 0x2           # v2/v3 = 2L
    div-long/2addr v0, v2           # v0/v1 = v0/v1 / 2
    long-to-int v2, v0              # v2 = (int) result, just to show the conversion
    return-wide v0
.end method

sections.title: Division by zero
sections.body: div-int, rem-int, div-long, rem-long and their /2addr and literal forms throw ArithmeticException when the divisor is zero. Floating-point division never throws: dividing by 0.0 produces Infinity or NaN, following IEEE 754. Note also that rem-float and rem-double are defined like Java's % operator (a - roundTowardZero(a / b) * b), not as the IEEE remainder.

exercises.prompt: Implement static int toFahrenheit(int c) that returns c * 9 / 5 + 32. Use the /lit8 forms so that every instruction takes a single register plus a constant.
exercises.starterCode:
.method public static toFahrenheit(I)I
    .registers 2
    # p0 = c
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method public static toFahrenheit(I)I
    .registers 2
    mul-int/lit8 v0, p0, 0x9
    div-int/lit8 v0, v0, 0x5
    add-int/lit8 v0, v0, 0x20
    return v0
.end method
exercises.hint: 9, 5 and 32 all fit in a signed 8-bit literal (-128..127).

exercises.prompt: Rewrite each instruction in its shorter /2addr form where that preserves the meaning. Leave any instruction that cannot be rewritten as it is and explain why in a comment.
exercises.starterCode:
add-int v0, v0, v1
mul-int v2, v2, v3
sub-int v4, v5, v4
exercises.solution:
add-int/2addr v0, v1
mul-int/2addr v2, v3
# sub-int v4, v5, v4 stays: the destination is the second operand and subtraction
# is not commutative, so v4 = v4 - v5 would compute a different value.
sub-int v4, v5, v4
exercises.hint: /2addr always computes vA = vA op vB.

exercises.prompt: Write static long sum(long a, long b) returning a + b. Work out how many parameter registers the method has before choosing the .registers value.
exercises.solution:
.method public static sum(JJ)J
    .registers 4
    # p0/p1 = a, p2/p3 = b; no extra locals needed
    add-long/2addr p0, p2
    return-wide p0
.end method
exercises.hint: Each long parameter takes two registers, so the parameters alone need four.

quiz.question: Which instruction computes 10 - v1 and stores it in v0?
quiz.explanation: rsub-int/lit8 computes literal minus register. sub-int/lit8 does not exist, and add-int/lit8 v0, v1, -0xa computes v1 - 10, the opposite subtraction.

quiz.question: If v1 holds 1 and v2 holds 33, what does v0 contain afterwards?
quiz.explanation: Int shifts use only the low 5 bits of the distance: 33 & 0x1f is 1, so the result is 1 << 1 = 2. The register is 32-bit, so a 64-bit result is impossible.

quiz.question: What happens when this runs with v2 = 0?
quiz.explanation: Integer division and remainder throw ArithmeticException for a zero divisor. The verifier cannot know a register's runtime value, so the code is valid; only float and double division return Infinity or NaN instead of throwing.

quiz.question: Which registers does add-long v0, v2, v4 read and write?
options: Writes v0 and v1; reads v2, v3, v4 and v5
Writes v0; reads v2 and v4
Writes v0 and v1; reads v2 and v4
quiz.explanation: A long occupies a register pair named by its lower register. Destination and both sources are pairs, so six registers are involved.

quiz.question: Why can add-int/2addr not be used when the destination is v16?
options: Its registers are 4-bit fields, so only v0 to v15 can be encoded
v16 is reserved for wide values
quiz.explanation: /2addr uses format 12x, which packs two 4-bit register numbers into one code unit. For higher registers the compiler must use the three-register 23x form.

lessons.title: Object Creation
lessons.summary: Creating an object in Dalvik takes two steps: new-instance allocates it and invoke-direct runs a constructor. Learn the uninitialised-reference rule, how constructors chain to their superclass, and how check-cast and instance-of work with the objects you create.

sections.title: Allocate, then initialise
sections.body:
The Java expression new Point(1, 2) is a single step in source code but two instructions in bytecode. new-instance vAA, type allocates an object of a (non-array) class and stores the reference in vAA. The object is not yet usable: its fields hold default values and no constructor has run. Next, invoke-direct calls one of the class's <init> methods, passing the new reference as the first argument, followed by the constructor arguments.

Until that constructor call happens, the verifier treats the reference as uninitialised. You may copy it or pass it to <init>, but calling any other method on it, storing it in a field, or returning it is rejected with a VerifyError.

sections.title: A class, its constructor and a factory
sections.body:
.class public Lcom/acme/demo/Point;
.super Ljava/lang/Object;

.field private final x:I
.field private final y:I

.method public constructor <init>(II)V
    .registers 3
    # p0 = this, p1 = x, p2 = y
    invoke-direct {p0}, Ljava/lang/Object;-><init>()V
    iput p1, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Point;->x:I
    iput p2, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Point;->y:I
    return-void
.end method

.method public static origin()Lcom/acme/demo/Point;
    .registers 2
    new-instance v0, Lcom/acme/demo/Point;
    const/4 v1, 0x0
    invoke-direct {v0, v1, v1}, Lcom/acme/demo/Point;-><init>(II)V
    return-object v0
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
Constructor chaining
sections.body:
Constructors are methods named <init> with a void return type, flagged with the constructor access flag. Inside a constructor, this (p0) also starts out uninitialised: before using it for anything else, the constructor must call another constructor on it, either one of its own class (this(...)) or one of the direct superclass (super(...)). That call is an invoke-direct to the superclass's <init>, not invoke-super, because constructors are never dispatched virtually.

Static initialisers are different: <clinit>()V is a static constructor that runs once when the class is initialised and never receives a this register.

sections.title: Calling the superclass constructor
instance-of and check-cast
sections.body: Once you have an object, two instructions check its type. instance-of vA, vB, type stores 1 in vA if the reference in vB is an instance of the type and 0 otherwise (null gives 0). check-cast vAA, type throws ClassCastException if the reference cannot be cast; null always passes. After a successful check-cast, the verifier treats the register as having the new type, which is why compilers emit it before calling a method that only exists on the subtype.

sections.title: Type test before a cast
sections.body:
.method public static lengthOrMinusOne(Ljava/lang/Object;)I
    .registers 2
    instance-of v0, p0, Ljava/lang/String;
    if-eqz v0, :not_string
    check-cast p0, Ljava/lang/String;
    invoke-virtual {p0}, Ljava/lang/String;->length()I
    move-result v0
    return v0

    :not_string
    const/4 v0, -0x1
    return v0
.end method

sections.title: Spotting StringBuilder chains
sections.body: String concatenation is a common source of object creation. For "x=" + x, D8 typically emits a StringBuilder chain: new-instance, invoke-direct <init>, one append per piece (each followed by move-result-object), then toString(). Recognising that pattern lets you read concatenations at a glance.

exercises.prompt: Write static java.util.List make() that creates and returns a new java.util.ArrayList.
exercises.hint: Allocate with new-instance, then call the no-argument <init> with invoke-direct.

exercises.prompt: This code assembles but fails verification when the class is loaded. Find the problem and fix it.
exercises.hint: Which instruction must run before any other method is called on a freshly allocated object?

exercises.prompt: Write static String label(int x) that returns "x=" + x using a StringBuilder. Use the StringBuilder(String) constructor to pass the prefix.
exercises.hint: append(I) returns the same builder, so you can keep it in v0 with move-result-object.

quiz.question: Which instruction calls a constructor on a newly allocated object?
quiz.explanation: Constructors are direct methods: they are never dispatched through the vtable, so both new Foo() and super(...) calls use invoke-direct on <init>.

quiz.question: What is wrong with this sequence?
options: toString() is called on an object whose constructor has not run
invoke-virtual cannot be used on v0
Nothing; it returns a valid string
quiz.explanation: After new-instance the reference is uninitialised. The verifier only allows it to be passed to <init>; calling toString() first causes a VerifyError.

quiz.question: What does instance-of store when the source register holds null?
quiz.explanation: null is not an instance of any type, so instance-of stores 0. check-cast, in contrast, lets null pass without throwing.

quiz.question: Which type can new-instance not allocate?
quiz.explanation: new-instance requires a non-array class. Arrays are created with new-array or filled-new-array.

quiz.question: In a subclass constructor, what must happen before this (p0) is used for anything else?
options: Another constructor of this class or the direct superclass must be invoked on p0
Nothing; p0 is fully initialised on entry
quiz.explanation: this starts uninitialised inside <init>. The verifier requires a call to this(...) or the superclass's <init> on p0 before it can be used like a normal object, for example to call its methods or return it.

lessons.title: Return Instructions
lessons.summary: Four instructions end a method: return-void, return, return-wide and return-object. Learn how to pick the one that matches the method's return type, how constructors return, and why compilers often route several branches through one shared exit.

sections.title: Choosing the right return
Wide and boolean returns
sections.body:
.method public static twice(J)J
    .registers 4
    # p0/p1 = value
    add-long v0, p0, p0
    return-wide v0
.end method

.method public static isEmpty(Ljava/lang/String;)Z
    .registers 2
    invoke-virtual {p0}, Ljava/lang/String;->length()I
    move-result v0
    if-nez v0, :not_empty
    const/4 v0, 0x1
    return v0

    :not_empty
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    return v0
.end method
A boolean is just an int that is 0 or 1, so it is returned with plain return. Returning null from a method with a reference return type uses const/4 v0, 0x0 followed by return-object v0.

sections.title: Multiple returns or one exit
sections.body: A method may contain any number of return instructions, and every path through the code must end in one (or in throw or an infinite loop): execution is not allowed to run past the last instruction. Some compilers return directly from each branch; others assign the result to a register and jump to a single exit block. Both are valid, and you will see both styles in real apps.

sections.title: A shared exit block
sections.body:
.method public static sign(I)I
    .registers 2
    if-lez p0, :not_positive
    const/4 v0, 0x1
    goto :exit

    :not_positive
    if-nez p0, :negative
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    goto :exit

    :negative
    const/4 v0, -0x1

    :exit
    return v0
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
Do not fall off the end
sections.body: Forgetting return-void at the end of a constructor or void method is a classic hand-editing mistake. The assembler accepts it, but the verifier reports that control flow falls off the end of the code.

exercises.prompt: This method should return 4294967296L. Fix the return instruction.
exercises.starterCode:
.method public static big()J
    .registers 2
    const-wide v0, 0x100000000L
    return v0
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method public static big()J
    .registers 2
    const-wide v0, 0x100000000L
    return-wide v0
.end method
exercises.hint: The return type J is 64 bits wide.

exercises.prompt: Write static String choose(boolean b) that returns "yes" when b is true and null otherwise.
exercises.solution:
.method public static choose(Z)Ljava/lang/String;
    .registers 2
    if-eqz p0, :no
    const-string v0, "yes"
    return-object v0

    :no
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    return-object v0
.end method
exercises.hint: null is the constant 0 returned with return-object.

exercises.prompt: This constructor fails verification. What is missing? Write the corrected method.
exercises.starterCode:
.method public constructor <init>()V
    .registers 1
    invoke-direct {p0}, Ljava/lang/Object;-><init>()V
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method public constructor <init>()V
    .registers 1
    invoke-direct {p0}, Ljava/lang/Object;-><init>()V
    return-void
.end method
exercises.hint: Constructors have the return type V.

quiz.question: Which instruction returns a double?
quiz.explanation: double and long are 64-bit values held in a register pair, returned with return-wide. return-double does not exist.

quiz.question: A method is declared ()[I. Which return instruction does it use?
quiz.explanation: Arrays are references, so even an int array is returned with return-object.

quiz.question: How does a constructor return?
quiz.explanation: <init> methods have the return type V. The new object is already in the caller's register from new-instance, so nothing is returned.

quiz.question: What happens with this method?
quiz.code:
.method public static one()J
    .registers 1
    const/4 v0, 0x1
    return v0
.end method
options: It assembles, but the verifier rejects it
The assembler refuses to build it
It returns 1 and the caller ignores the upper half
quiz.explanation: The assembler does not check types. At class load the verifier sees a 32-bit return in a method whose prototype returns J and throws VerifyError.

quiz.question: Which statement about return instructions is true?
options: A method may contain several return instructions
Only the last instruction of a method may be a return
return can only use registers v0 to v15
return-void is optional at the end of void methods
quiz.explanation: Any branch may return. The return opcodes use format 11x with an 8-bit register, and control must never fall off the end of a method.

lessons.title: Exception Handling
lessons.summary: Smali marks protected code with try labels and attaches handlers with .catch and .catchall. Learn how move-exception and throw work, how handlers are ordered, why finally blocks appear twice, and how synchronized blocks use a catch-all handler to release their monitor.

sections.title: Try ranges and handlers
sections.body:
In a .dex file, exception handling is a table attached to the method's code: each entry covers a range of instructions and lists handler addresses for exception types. Smali writes that table with labels. You place a start label and an end label around the protected instructions and then declare a handler:

.catch Ljava/io/IOException; {:try_start_0 .. :try_end_0} :catch_0

.catchall {:try_start_0 .. :try_end_0} :catchall_0 does the same for every Throwable. The label names are free to choose; baksmali simply generates try_start_N, try_end_N and catch_N.

sections.title: Catching an exception
sections.body:
.method public static parseOrDefault(Ljava/lang/String;I)I
    .registers 3
    # p0 = text, p1 = fallback
    :try_start_0
    invoke-static {p0}, Ljava/lang/Integer;->parseInt(Ljava/lang/String;)I
    move-result v0
    :try_end_0
    .catch Ljava/lang/NumberFormatException; {:try_start_0 .. :try_end_0} :catch_0

    return v0

    :catch_0
    move-exception v0
    return p1
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
Handler order, move-exception and throw
sections.body:
When an exception is thrown inside a covered range, the runtime checks that range's handlers in the order they are listed and jumps to the first one whose type matches; a catch-all handler is always considered last. List more specific types first: a catch for IOException placed before one for FileNotFoundException would swallow both.

move-exception vAA copies the caught exception into a register. It must be the very first instruction of a handler, and it is not allowed anywhere else; a handler that does not need the exception object can omit it. throw vAA raises the exception held in a register, which can be one you just created or one you caught.

sections.title: Creating and throwing an exception
sections.body:
.method public static requirePositive(I)I
    .registers 3
    if-lez p0, :bad
    return p0

    :bad
    new-instance v0, Ljava/lang/IllegalArgumentException;
    const-string v1, "value must be positive"
    invoke-direct {v0, v1}, Ljava/lang/IllegalArgumentException;-><init>(Ljava/lang/String;)V
    throw v0
.end method

sections.title: finally and synchronized
sections.body:
Dalvik has no instruction for finally. The compiler copies the finally code onto every exit path:
once after the protected code for normal completion and once in a catch-all handler that runs the cleanup and rethrows. Seeing the same calls twice is therefore expected, not a bug.

synchronized blocks follow the same idea. monitor-enter acquires the lock, the body is covered by a catch-all, and both the normal path and the handler execute monitor-exit before leaving. Compilers usually protect the handler's own monitor-exit too, so the lock is released even if that step faults. try-with-resources expands into the same building blocks: nested try ranges, a call to close() on each path, and addSuppressed() when close() throws during an exception.

sections.title: synchronized (this) { count++; }
sections.body:
.method public increment()V
    .registers 3
    monitor-enter p0
    :try_start_0
    iget v0, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->count:I
    add-int/lit8 v0, v0, 0x1
    iput v0, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->count:I
    monitor-exit p0
    :try_end_0
    .catchall {:try_start_0 .. :try_end_0} :catchall_0
    return-void

    :catchall_0
    move-exception v1
    :try_start_1
    monitor-exit p0
    :try_end_1
    .catchall {:try_start_1 .. :try_end_1} :catchall_0
    throw v1
.end method

sections.title: Labels define the protection
sections.body: When editing smali, keep every instruction that can throw inside the intended try range and do not move labels casually. Code placed between :try_end and the handler is not protected, and an instruction other than move-exception at the start of a handler that uses the exception makes the method fail verification.

exercises.prompt: Write static boolean pause(long millis) that calls Thread.sleep(millis) and returns true, or returns false if an InterruptedException is caught.
exercises.solution:
.method public static pause(J)Z
    .registers 4
    # p0/p1 = millis
    :try_start_0
    invoke-static {p0, p1}, Ljava/lang/Thread;->sleep(J)V
    :try_end_0
    .catch Ljava/lang/InterruptedException; {:try_start_0 .. :try_end_0} :catch_0

    const/4 v0, 0x1
    return v0

    :catch_0
    move-exception v0
    const/4 v1, 0x0
    return v1
.end method
exercises.hint: A long argument is passed as both registers of its pair: {p0, p1}.

exercises.prompt: The handler below fails verification. Explain why and fix it.
exercises.starterCode:
.method public static safeLength(Ljava/lang/String;)I
    .registers 3
    :try_start_0
    invoke-virtual {p0}, Ljava/lang/String;->length()I
    move-result v0
    :try_end_0
    .catch Ljava/lang/NullPointerException; {:try_start_0 .. :try_end_0} :catch_0
    return v0

    :catch_0
    const/4 v1, 0x0
    move-exception v0
    return v1
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method public static safeLength(Ljava/lang/String;)I
    .registers 3
    :try_start_0
    invoke-virtual {p0}, Ljava/lang/String;->length()I
    move-result v0
    :try_end_0
    .catch Ljava/lang/NullPointerException; {:try_start_0 .. :try_end_0} :catch_0
    return v0

    # move-exception must be the first instruction of the handler
    :catch_0
    move-exception v0
    const/4 v1, 0x0
    return v1
.end method
exercises.hint: Look at the order of the first two instructions after :catch_0.

exercises.prompt: Write the instructions that throw new IllegalStateException("closed"). Assume v0 and v1 are free.
exercises.solution:
new-instance v0, Ljava/lang/IllegalStateException;
const-string v1, "closed"
invoke-direct {v0, v1}, Ljava/lang/IllegalStateException;-><init>(Ljava/lang/String;)V
throw v0
exercises.hint: Allocate, call the (Ljava/lang/String;)V constructor, then throw the register.

quiz.question: Where may move-exception appear?
options: Only as the first instruction of an exception handler
Only at the end of a method
quiz.explanation: The bytecode rules require move-exception to be the first instruction of a handler and forbid it everywhere else. Handlers that ignore the exception can leave it out.

quiz.question: Both handlers cover the same range. Which one runs for a FileNotFoundException?
quiz.code:
:try_start_0
invoke-virtual {p0}, Ljava/io/InputStream;->read()I
:try_end_0
.catch Ljava/io/IOException; {:try_start_0 .. :try_end_0} :catch_io
.catch Ljava/io/FileNotFoundException; {:try_start_0 .. :try_end_0} :catch_missing
return-void

:catch_io
return-void

:catch_missing
return-void
options: :catch_io, because handlers are checked in the listed order
:catch_missing, because it is the most specific type
Neither; the verifier rejects overlapping handlers
quiz.explanation: FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException. The first matching handler wins, so specific types must be listed before their superclasses.

quiz.question: Why does the cleanup call of a finally block often appear twice in smali?
options: The compiler copies it onto the normal path and into a catch-all handler that rethrows
baksmali duplicates code to make it easier to read
One copy is for 32-bit and one for 64-bit devices
quiz.explanation: Dalvik has no finally instruction. Compilers inline the finally code on each exit path, using a .catchall handler for the exceptional one.

quiz.question: What does .catchall catch?
options: Any Throwable thrown in its range
Only exceptions thrown with the throw instruction
quiz.explanation: A catch-all handler has no type and matches every Throwable, including errors and exceptions raised by the runtime itself, such as NullPointerException.

quiz.question: In a synchronized block, why is the body covered by a .catchall handler?
options: So that monitor-exit runs and the lock is released even when the body throws
Because monitor-enter cannot be used without one
To convert checked exceptions into unchecked ones
To retry the body after an exception
quiz.explanation: The handler calls monitor-exit on the same object and rethrows the exception, mirroring the guarantee that leaving a synchronized block always releases its lock.

lessons.title: DEX Structure
lessons.summary: Look inside a classes.dex file: the 0x70-byte header, the sorted ID tables that every class, field, method and string reference points into, the data section and the map_list that describes it all. You will learn how a line of smali turns into table indices.

sections.title: One file, shared tables
sections.body:
A .dex file is a single container for many classes. Instead of every class carrying its own constant pool (as JVM .class files do), all classes in the file share a set of de-duplicated tables. The file is laid out in this order:
- header
- string_ids, type_ids, proto_ids, field_ids, method_ids, class_defs
- call_site_ids and method_handles (DEX version 038 and later)
- data (everything the tables point at)
- link_data (unspecified, empty in normal app files)

All multi-byte values are little-endian. Most tables are arrays of fixed-size items, so the n-th entry can be found with simple arithmetic: offset + n * item size.

sections.title: The header
sections.body:
The header_item starts at offset 0 and, for format versions up to 040, is exactly 0x70 (112) bytes long:
- 0x00 magic: 8 bytes, "dex\n" followed by a three-digit version and a zero byte, e.g. 64 65 78 0a 30 33 39 00 for "dex\n039\0".
- 0x08 checksum: Adler-32 of everything after this field (the whole file minus magic and checksum).
- 0x0C signature: 20-byte SHA-1 of everything after the signature field.
- 0x20 file_size, 0x24 header_size (0x70), 0x28 endian_tag (0x12345678, stored as 78 56 34 12).
- 0x2C link_size, 0x30 link_off, 0x34 map_off.
- 0x38 to 0x67: size/offset pairs for string_ids, type_ids, proto_ids, field_ids, method_ids and class_defs.
- 0x68 data_size, 0x6C data_off.

The version tells you which features may appear: 035 is the classic format, 037 arrived with Android 7.0 (default interface methods), 038 with Android 8.0 (invoke-polymorphic, invoke-custom, method handles, call sites), 039 with Android 9 (const-method-handle, const-method-type) and 040 with Android 10 (wider SimpleName character set). Version 041, an experimental container format in Android 16, enlarges the header to 0x78 bytes.

sections.title: The ID tables
sections.body:
Each ID table is sorted and free of duplicates, which lets tools binary-search them:
- string_id_item (4 bytes): offset of a string_data_item, which holds a ULEB128 UTF-16 length followed by MUTF-8 bytes and a terminating 0. Sorted by string contents.
- type_id_item (4 bytes): descriptor_idx, an index into string_ids such as "Ljava/lang/String;".
- proto_id_item (12 bytes): shorty_idx, return_type_idx and parameters_off (a type_list, or 0).
- field_id_item (8 bytes): class_idx (ushort), type_idx (ushort), name_idx (uint).
- method_id_item (8 bytes): class_idx (ushort), proto_idx (ushort), name_idx (uint).
- class_def_item (32 bytes): class_idx, access_flags, superclass_idx, interfaces_off, source_file_idx, annotations_off, class_data_off, static_values_off.
- call_site_id_item (4 bytes) and method_handle_item (8 bytes) for the invoke-custom and method-handle features.

class_defs has one extra rule: a superclass or implemented interface defined in the same file must appear before the classes that extend it.

sections.title: Every reference becomes an index
sections.body:
.class public Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;
.super Ljava/lang/Object;
.source "Counter.java"

# field_ids entry: class_idx -> Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;, type_idx -> I, name_idx -> "count"
.field private count:I

.method public increment()V
    .registers 3

    # field@ index into field_ids
    iget v0, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->count:I
    add-int/lit8 v0, v0, 0x1
    iput v0, p0, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->count:I

    # string@ index into string_ids
    const-string v1, "Counter"

    # meth@ index into method_ids; its proto_idx points at the shorty "VL"
    invoke-static {v1}, Lcom/acme/demo/Counter;->log(Ljava/lang/String;)V
    return-void
.end method

.method private static log(Ljava/lang/String;)V
    .registers 1
    return-void
.end method

sections.title: The data section and map_list
sections.body:
The data section holds everything variable-sized: class_data_item (the field and method lists of a class, ULEB128-encoded), code_item (registers_size, ins_size, outs_size, tries_size, debug_info_off, insns_size and the instructions themselves), string data, type_lists, annotation structures, encoded arrays with static field initial values and debug info.

map_list, found at header.map_off inside the data section, is a table of contents for the whole file. Each 12-byte map_item records a type code (0x0000 header_item, 0x0001 string_id_item, 0x1000 map_list, 0x2001 code_item and so on), an item count and an offset. Entries are ordered by offset and never overlap, which makes map_list the easiest way to walk a file you know nothing about.

link_data is reserved for statically linked files; its format is left to the runtime and it is empty in the dex files produced by D8 and R8.

sections.title: Where the 64K limit comes from
sections.body: Instructions such as invoke-* and the field accessors encode their reference as a 16-bit index (meth@BBBB, field@CCCC). A single dex file can therefore reference at most 65,536 methods, which is why large apps are split into classes.dex, classes2.dex and so on (multidex). Strings have an escape hatch: const-string/jumbo takes a 32-bit string index.

sections.title: Checksums matter
sections.body: Patching bytes in a .dex file by hand invalidates the checksum and signature. Reassembling with smali (or any dex writer) recomputes both; a stale checksum makes tools and the runtime treat the file as corrupt.

exercises.prompt: A file starts with the bytes 64 65 78 0a 30 33 38 00. Which format version is it, and which instructions might you find in it that a 035 file cannot contain?
exercises.solution:
The magic decodes to "dex\n038\0", so this is version 038 (introduced with Android 8.0). It may
contain invoke-polymorphic, invoke-polymorphic/range, invoke-custom and invoke-custom/range,
together with call_site_ids and method_handles tables. const-method-handle and const-method-type
need version 039.
exercises.hint: Bytes 0x30-0x39 are the ASCII digits '0'-'9'.

exercises.prompt:
List every ID table that is touched when the runtime resolves this instruction:
invoke-virtual {v0, v1}, Ljava/lang/StringBuilder;->append(Ljava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/StringBuilder;
exercises.solution:
meth@ selects a method_id_item. Its class_idx points into type_ids (Ljava/lang/StringBuilder;),
whose descriptor_idx points into string_ids. Its name_idx points into string_ids ("append"). Its
proto_idx points into proto_ids, whose shorty_idx is the string "LL", whose return_type_idx is
the StringBuilder type, and whose parameters_off leads to a type_list containing the type id of
Ljava/lang/String;. So: method_ids, type_ids, proto_ids and string_ids (plus a type_list in the
data section).
exercises.hint: Follow class_idx, proto_idx and name_idx, then follow what each of those points to.

exercises.prompt: A huge generated class has more than 65,536 distinct strings. Write a static method banner()Ljava/lang/String; that loads the string "Welcome" with an instruction that works no matter how large the string index becomes.
exercises.solution:
.method public static banner()Ljava/lang/String;
    .registers 1
    const-string/jumbo v0, "Welcome"
    return-object v0
.end method
exercises.hint: const-string uses a 16-bit index (format 21c); its jumbo variant uses format 31c.

quiz.question: What is the value of header_size in a version 035-040 dex file?
options: It varies with the number of classes
quiz.explanation: The header is a fixed 0x70 bytes up to version 040. Only the experimental 041 container format grows it to 0x78 bytes to add container_size and header_offset.

quiz.question: What does the header's checksum field hold?
options: An Adler-32 checksum of the file after the checksum field
A SHA-1 hash of the whole file
A CRC-32 of the data section only
quiz.explanation: checksum is Adler-32 over everything except magic and checksum itself. The separate 20-byte signature field is a SHA-1 hash over everything after the signature.

quiz.question: Which three fields make up a method_id_item?
quiz.explanation: A method_id_item is 8 bytes: the defining class (ushort index into type_ids), the prototype (ushort index into proto_ids) and the name (uint index into string_ids). Access flags and code live in class_data_item, not in the ID table.

quiz.question: What does the operand of this instruction refer to inside the dex file?
options: An index into the string_ids table
A byte offset to the string inside the instruction stream
A pointer into the APK's resources.arsc
quiz.explanation: const-string encodes string@BBBB, a 16-bit index into string_ids. The string_id_item then points to the MUTF-8 string data in the data section.

quiz.question: Where is the map_list stored?
options: In the data section, at the offset given by header.map_off
Immediately after the header, before string_ids
At the very end of link_data
quiz.explanation: map_off must be non-zero and point into the data section. The map lists every section with its type, item count and offset, ordered by offset.

quiz.question: Which dex format version first allowed invoke-custom and method handles?
quiz.explanation: Version 038 (Android 8.0) added invoke-polymorphic, invoke-custom, call sites and method handles. 039 (Android 9) added the const-method-handle and const-method-type instructions.

lessons.title: Instruction Encoding
lessons.summary: Learn how Dalvik instructions are packed into 16-bit code units, how to read format ids such as 12x, 22c, 35c and 51l, and how to encode and decode instructions by hand. You will also see why payload tables must be aligned.

sections.title: Code units
sections.body:
A method's bytecode (code_item.insns) is an array of 16-bit code units, stored little-endian. Every instruction occupies one or more whole code units, and the opcode is always the low 8 bits of the first unit. The remaining 8 bits of that first unit, and any following units, hold operands.

Sizes and branch offsets are always counted in code units, not bytes: an instruction at address 3 with a length of 2 is followed by the instruction at address 5.

sections.title: Reading format ids
sections.body:
Every opcode has a format, named by a short id:
- First digit: number of code units (1-5).
- Second digit: maximum number of registers, or "r" for a register range.
- Final letter: kind of extra data. x = none, n = 4-bit literal, b = 8-bit literal, s = 16-bit literal, h = 16-bit literal holding high-order bits, i = 32-bit literal, l = 64-bit literal, t = branch target, c = constant pool index. 45cc and 4rcc carry two pool indices.

The bitwise layout reads high bits to low; each letter is 4 bits and "op" is the 8-bit opcode:
- 10x  ØØ|op                       e.g. return-void, nop
- 12x  B|A|op                      e.g. move vA, vB; add-int/2addr
- 11n  B|A|op                      const/4 vA, #+B
- 21s  AA|op BBBB                  const/16 vAA, #+BBBB
- 22c  B|A|op CCCC                 iget vA, vB, field@CCCC
- 23x  AA|op CC|BB                 add-int vAA, vBB, vCC
- 35c  A|G|op BBBB F|E|D|C         invoke-* with up to 5 argument registers
- 3rc  AA|op BBBB CCCC             invoke-*/range {vCCCC .. vNNNN}
- 45cc A|G|op BBBB F|E|D|C HHHH    invoke-polymorphic (method + proto)
- 51l  AA|op BBBB BBBB BBBB BBBB   const-wide vAA, 64-bit literal

sections.title: Formats in a real method
sections.body:
.method public static demo(II)I
    .registers 6

    const/4 v0, 0x1                 # 11n: 1 code unit
    const/16 v1, 0x2a               # 21s: 2 code units
    add-int v2, p0, p1              # 23x: 2 code units
    add-int/2addr v2, v0            # 12x: 1 code unit
    const-wide v0, 0x123456789L     # 51l: 5 code units (v0 and v1 hold the long)
    invoke-static {p0, p1}, Ljava/lang/Math;->max(II)I   # 35c: 3 code units
    move-result v0                  # 11x: 1 code unit
    return v0                       # 11x: 1 code unit
.end method

sections.title: Encoding by hand
sections.body:
Encode const/4 v0, 1. Format 11n is B|A|op with op = 0x12, A = 0 (register) and B = 1 (literal), giving the code unit 0x1012, stored in the file as the bytes 12 10.

return-void is format 10x with op 0x0e: the unit 0x000e, bytes 0e 00.

add-int v0, v1, v2 uses 23x (AA|op CC|BB). Unit one is 0x0090 (AA = 0, op = 0x90); unit two is 0x0201 (CC = 2 in the high byte, BB = 1 in the low byte). Bytes: 90 00 01 02.

add-int/2addr v1, v2 is 12x: B = 2, A = 1, op = 0xb0, so 0x21b0, bytes b0 21.

invoke-virtual {v1, v2}, meth@0005 is 35c (op 0x6e). The first unit packs A = 2 (argument count) and G = 0 above the opcode: 0x206e. The second unit is the method index 0x0005. The third unit is F|E|D|C = 0|0|2|1, i.e. 0x0021. Bytes: 6e 20 05 00 21 00.

sections.title: Why 4-bit fields matter
sections.body: Formats with 4-bit register fields (12x, 11n, 22c, 22t, 35c and others) can only name v0-v15. The assembler refuses move v1, v20 with "Must be between v0 and v15", so you need move/from16, and invoke-* calls whose arguments sit in high or many registers need the /range form. This is why compilers try hard to keep hot values in low registers.

sections.title: Payloads and alignment
sections.body:
The data tables used by packed-switch, sparse-switch and fill-array-data are pseudo-instructions identified by the first unit 0x0100, 0x0200 or 0x0300. They must start at an even code-unit offset (4-byte aligned), so dex writers insert a nop before a payload when needed. Their sizes in code units are:
- packed-switch-payload: size * 2 + 4
- sparse-switch-payload: size * 4 + 2
- fill-array-data-payload: (size * element_width + 1) / 2 + 4

Payloads are never executed; they are normally placed after the method's last real instruction.

Branch offsets (+AA, +AAAA, +AAAAAAAA) are signed and relative to the address of the branching instruction itself, measured in code units. Mixing up bytes and code units, or measuring from the next instruction, is the most common hand-encoding mistake.

exercises.prompt: Hand-encode const/4 v3, -1. Give the 16-bit code unit and the two bytes as they appear in the file.
exercises.solution:
Format 11n: B|A|op. -1 as a signed 4-bit value is 0xF, A = 3, op = 0x12. The code unit is
0xF312 and the little-endian bytes are 12 f3.
exercises.hint: Literals in 11n are 4-bit two's complement, so the range is -8..7.

exercises.prompt: Decode the bytes 90 02 03 04 into a smali instruction.
exercises.solution:
Unit one is 0x0290: opcode 0x90 (add-int, format 23x) with AA = 2. Unit two is 0x0403: BB is
the low byte (3) and CC the high byte (4). The instruction is add-int v2, v3, v4.
exercises.hint: Remember that each unit is little-endian and 23x stores CC|BB, high byte first in the layout.

exercises.prompt: This method does not assemble because move uses format 12x. Fix it without changing which registers are read and written.
exercises.starterCode:
.method public static copy()V
    .registers 21
    move v1, v20
    return-void
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method public static copy()V
    .registers 21
    move/from16 v1, v20
    return-void
.end method
exercises.hint: move/from16 (format 22x) takes an 8-bit destination and a 16-bit source register.

quiz.question: What does the format id 22c tell you?
options: 2 code units, up to 2 registers, a constant pool index
2 registers, 2 code units, a branch target
A compressed format used only by odex files
quiz.explanation: First digit = code units, second digit = register count, letter c = constant pool index. 22c is used by iget/iput (field@CCCC), instance-of and new-array (type@CCCC).

quiz.question: What is the 16-bit code unit for this instruction?
quiz.explanation: const/4 is opcode 0x12 in format 11n (B|A|op). B = 1, A = 0, so the unit is 0x1012, written to the file as the bytes 12 10.

quiz.question: How many argument registers can a 35c invoke list hold?
quiz.explanation: 35c has a 4-bit count A and five 4-bit register fields C, D, E, F, G. Calls needing more argument words, or registers above v15, use the 3rc /range form.

quiz.question: Which format holds a full 64-bit literal?
quiz.explanation: 51l (used by const-wide) is 5 code units: the opcode unit plus four units of literal. 21h holds only the high 16 bits (const-wide/high16) and 31i a 32-bit value.

quiz.question: Why might a dex writer emit a nop just before a packed-switch-payload?
options: Payloads must start at an even code-unit offset (4-byte aligned)
The verifier requires a nop before every label
To give the switch somewhere to fall through
nop marks the end of the method
quiz.explanation: Payload pseudo-instructions must be 4-byte aligned. If the previous instruction ends at an odd code-unit offset, a one-unit nop pads the gap.

lessons.title: Method References
lessons.summary: Understand what a method reference really is in a dex file: a method_id with a class, a name and a prototype with its shorty. Then go beyond classic calls with method handles, invoke-polymorphic and invoke-custom call sites introduced in Android 8.0.

sections.title: Anatomy of a method reference
sections.body:
In smali a method reference looks like Ljava/util/List;->get(I)Ljava/lang/Object;. In the dex file it is a method_id_item made of three indices:
- class_idx: the type the reference names (Ljava/util/List;),
- name_idx: the method name ("get"),
- proto_idx: a proto_id_item describing parameters and return type.

A proto_id_item stores the return type, a type_list of parameters, and a shorty: a compact string with the return type first and one character per parameter, where every reference type (objects and arrays alike) collapses to L. (Ljava/lang/String;I[J)Z has the shorty ZLIL.

The class in a reference is the type the compiler saw at the call site, not necessarily the class that declares the code. Calling hashCode() on an ArrayList variable references Ljava/util/ArrayList;->hashCode()I, and the runtime resolves it by searching ArrayList and then its superclasses.

sections.title: Classic references
sections.body:
.method public static describe(Ljava/util/List;)Ljava/lang/String;
    .registers 3

    # interface reference: class_idx -> Ljava/util/List;, shorty "I"
    invoke-interface {p0}, Ljava/util/List;->size()I
    move-result v0

    # static reference: shorty "LI"
    invoke-static {v0}, Ljava/lang/Integer;->toString(I)Ljava/lang/String;
    move-result-object v1
    return-object v1
.end method

sections.title: Method handles and invoke-polymorphic
sections.body:
java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle (API 26) has two special methods, invoke and invokeExact. They are signature polymorphic: their declaration is a native varargs method taking Object[] and returning Object, but each call site may pass any argument types and expect any return type.

Dalvik models this with invoke-polymorphic (format 45cc) and invoke-polymorphic/range (4rcc). Each carries two references: meth@BBBB, the declared polymorphic method, and proto@HHHH, the actual prototype of this call. The first register is the receiver, the MethodHandle itself. Both instructions require dex version 038 (Android 8.0, API 26).

sections.title: invoke-polymorphic
sections.body:
.method public static apply(Ljava/lang/invoke/MethodHandle;II)I
    .registers 3

    # p0 = the handle (receiver), p1 and p2 = the int arguments
    # method: the declared signature-polymorphic method
    # proto (II)I: the types used at this call site
    invoke-polymorphic {p0, p1, p2}, Ljava/lang/invoke/MethodHandle;->invokeExact([Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/Object;, (II)I
    move-result v0
    return v0
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
invoke-custom and call sites
sections.body:
invoke-custom (format 35c) and invoke-custom/range (3rc) reference a call site rather than a method. A call_site_id points to a call_site_item: an encoded array whose first three values are a method handle for the bootstrap method, a method name and a method type, optionally followed by extra constant arguments.

The first time the instruction executes, the runtime calls the bootstrap method, which must return a java.lang.invoke.CallSite. The call site is then bound, and this and every later execution invokes the CallSite's target handle exactly, with the instruction's registers as arguments. Exceptions thrown during bootstrapping are wrapped in BootstrapMethodError. Like invoke-polymorphic, it needs dex 038.

sections.title: invoke-custom in smali
sections.body:
.method public static combine(II)I
    .registers 2

    # call_site_0: name "combine", type (II)I, one extra bootstrap argument (0x1)
    invoke-custom {p0, p1}, call_site_0("combine", (II)I, 0x1)@Lcom/acme/demo/Linker;->bootstrap(Ljava/lang/invoke/MethodHandles$Lookup;Ljava/lang/String;Ljava/lang/invoke/MethodType;I)Ljava/lang/invoke/CallSite;
    move-result v0
    return v0
.end method

You rarely see invoke-custom in ordinary app code: D8 and R8 normally desugar Java lambdas and string concatenation into plain classes and StringBuilder calls. It shows up in code built specifically for it, in some libraries, and in hand-written tests of the runtime.

exercises.prompt: Write the shorty for a method with the descriptor (J[Ljava/lang/String;D)V.
exercises.solution:
VJLD: return type V first, then J for the long, L for the String array (all reference types,
including arrays, become L) and D for the double.
exercises.hint: Return type first; arrays are references.

exercises.prompt: Write a static method length(Ljava/lang/invoke/MethodHandle;Ljava/lang/String;)I that calls invokeExact on the handle with the String argument and returns the int result.
exercises.solution:
.method public static length(Ljava/lang/invoke/MethodHandle;Ljava/lang/String;)I
    .registers 2
    invoke-polymorphic {p0, p1}, Ljava/lang/invoke/MethodHandle;->invokeExact([Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/Object;, (Ljava/lang/String;)I
    move-result v0
    return v0
.end method
exercises.hint: The proto describes the call site: one String in, int out. The receiver is not part of it.

exercises.prompt: Describe the method_id_item and proto_id_item behind Ljava/util/List;->size()I.
exercises.solution:
method_id_item: class_idx -> type_ids entry for Ljava/util/List;, name_idx -> string "size",
proto_idx -> a proto_id_item whose shorty is "I", whose return_type_idx is the type I and whose
parameters_off is 0 because there are no parameters.
exercises.hint: A prototype with no parameters has no type_list.

quiz.question: What is the shorty for (Ljava/lang/String;I[J)Z?
quiz.explanation: Return type first (Z), then one character per parameter. String becomes L, int is I, and the long array [J is a reference type, so it also becomes L.

quiz.question: In this instruction, what does (II)I describe?
options: The prototype of this particular call site
The types stored in v0-v2 before the call
quiz.explanation: proto@HHHH gives the argument and return types actually used at the call. The method reference keeps the declared polymorphic signature ([Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/Object;.

quiz.question: What happens the first time an invoke-custom instruction executes?
options: The bootstrap method runs and returns a CallSite that gets bound to the call site
The verifier rewrites it into invoke-static
The runtime looks up the method by name in the current class
It throws unless the call site was linked at install time
quiz.explanation: Call site resolution calls the bootstrap linker method with the values from call_site_item. The returned CallSite's target handle is then invoked with the instruction's arguments.

quiz.question: Which Android version first supports invoke-polymorphic and invoke-custom?
quiz.explanation: Both arrived with dex format 038 in Android 8.0. Android 9 and dex 039 added const-method-handle and const-method-type.

quiz.question: An exception thrown inside a bootstrap method surfaces as which error?
quiz.explanation: The dalvik-bytecode reference states that exceptions from the bootstrap linker method are wrapped in java.lang.BootstrapMethodError, which is also thrown if it returns no CallSite, a null target or a target of the wrong type.

lessons.title: Control Flow
lessons.summary:
Split methods into basic blocks, follow every kind of edge, and master the branch instructions:
the three goto widths, packed and sparse switches with their payload tables, and the shape the compilers produce for a switch on strings.

sections.title: Basic blocks and edges
sections.body:
A basic block is a straight run of instructions with one entry and one exit. A new block starts (a "leader") at:
- the first instruction of the method,
- every branch or switch target and every exception handler,
- the instruction after a goto, if-*, switch, return-* or throw.

Edges connect blocks: fall-through to the next block, the taken side of an if-*, one edge per switch case plus the fall-through default, and exceptional edges from any instruction that can throw inside a try range to its handlers. Drawing this graph is the fastest way to understand an unfamiliar method.

sections.title: Six blocks in one method
sections.body:
.method public static sign(I)I
    .registers 2

    # Block A: entry
    if-lez p0, :not_positive

    # Block B: fall-through of the if
    const/4 v0, 0x1
    goto :done

    # Block C: branch target
    :not_positive
    if-eqz p0, :zero

    # Block D
    const/4 v0, -0x1
    goto :done

    # Block E
    :zero
    const/4 v0, 0x0

    # Block F: join point reached from B, D and E
    :done
    return v0
.end method

sections.title: goto, goto/16 and goto/32
sections.body:
There are three unconditional jumps, differing only in offset width (offsets are signed, in code units, relative to the goto itself):
- goto (10t): 8-bit offset, -128..127
- goto/16 (20t): 16-bit offset, -32768..32767
- goto/32 (30t): 32-bit offset

goto and goto/16 may not have an offset of 0. goto/32 may, so it is the one form that can jump to itself; a spin loop can also be built with a nop as the target. Conditional branches (if-test and if-testz) always use a 16-bit offset, so they reach only about 32K code units in either direction. In smali you write labels and the assembler computes the offsets.

sections.title: packed-switch with its payload
sections.body:
.method public static price(I)I
    .registers 2

    packed-switch p0, :pswitch_data
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    return v0

    :pswitch_small
    const/16 v0, 0xa
    return v0

    :pswitch_medium
    const/16 v0, 0x14
    return v0

    :pswitch_large
    const/16 v0, 0x1e
    return v0

    # cases 1, 2, 3 in order
    :pswitch_data
    .packed-switch 0x1
        :pswitch_small
        :pswitch_medium
        :pswitch_large
    .end packed-switch
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
Choosing between packed and sparse
sections.body:
packed-switch suits dense case values: the payload stores first_key and one target per consecutive key (size * 2 + 4 code units). sparse-switch suits scattered values: the payload stores sorted keys and a matching target for each (size * 4 + 2 code units). In both, targets are relative to the address of the switch instruction, not the payload. When no case matches, execution falls through to the instruction right after the switch, which is where the default branch lives.

A switch on a String typically compiles in two steps: call hashCode(), sparse-switch on the hash, then confirm each candidate with equals() because different strings can share a hash. javac then switches a second time on a small index; D8 or R8 may simplify that shape, so expect variations.

sections.title: Switch on strings: hashCode, then equals
sections.body:
.method public static colorCode(Ljava/lang/String;)I
    .registers 3

    invoke-virtual {p0}, Ljava/lang/String;->hashCode()I
    move-result v0
    sparse-switch v0, :sswitch_data

    :no_match
    const/4 v0, -0x1
    return v0

    :sswitch_red
    const-string v1, "red"
    invoke-virtual {p0, v1}, Ljava/lang/String;->equals(Ljava/lang/Object;)Z
    move-result v1
    if-eqz v1, :no_match
    const/4 v0, 0x1
    return v0

    :sswitch_blue
    const-string v1, "blue"
    invoke-virtual {p0, v1}, Ljava/lang/String;->equals(Ljava/lang/Object;)Z
    move-result v1
    if-eqz v1, :no_match
    const/4 v0, 0x2
    return v0

    # keys are "red".hashCode() and "blue".hashCode(), sorted low to high
    :sswitch_data
    .sparse-switch
        0x1b891 -> :sswitch_red
        0x2e305a -> :sswitch_blue
    .end sparse-switch
.end method
When reading a big method, find the switch payloads at the bottom first: they list every case label, so they tell you where each case starts before you read a single case body.

exercises.prompt: Split this method into basic blocks and list the edges between them.
exercises.starterCode:
.method public static abs(I)I
    .registers 1
    if-gez p0, :positive
    neg-int p0, p0
    :positive
    return p0
.end method
exercises.solution:
Block 1: if-gez p0, :positive. Block 2: neg-int p0, p0 (leader because it follows a
conditional branch). Block 3: :positive return p0 (leader because it is a branch target).
Edges: 1 -> 3 (branch taken), 1 -> 2 (fall-through), 2 -> 3 (fall-through). Block 3 has no
successors because it returns.
exercises.hint: Leaders: the first instruction, branch targets, and instructions after a branch.

exercises.prompt: Write a static method weekdayHours(I)I that returns 8 for 0, 8 for 1 and 4 for 2, and 0 for any other value. Use a packed-switch.
exercises.solution:
.method public static weekdayHours(I)I
    .registers 2
    packed-switch p0, :pswitch_data
    const/4 v0, 0x0
    return v0
    :pswitch_full
    const/16 v0, 0x8
    return v0
    :pswitch_half
    const/4 v0, 0x4
    return v0
    :pswitch_data
    .packed-switch 0x0
        :pswitch_full
        :pswitch_full
        :pswitch_half
    .end packed-switch
.end method
exercises.hint: Two cases may share the same target label. 8 does not fit in const/4 (range -8..7).

exercises.prompt: How many code units do the payloads of a 5-case packed-switch and a 5-case sparse-switch occupy?
exercises.solution:
packed-switch-payload: 5 * 2 + 4 = 14 code units. sparse-switch-payload: 5 * 4 + 2 = 22 code
units. The sparse table is larger because it stores a key for every target.
exercises.hint: Each key and each target is a 32-bit int, which is two code units.

quiz.question: What offset range does goto/16 support?
quiz.explanation: goto/16 (format 20t) carries a signed 16-bit offset counted in code units. goto has 8 bits and goto/32 has 32 bits.

quiz.question: Which jump may legally use an offset of 0 (jump to itself)?
quiz.explanation: The bytecode reference forbids a zero offset for goto, goto/16 and the if-* branches. goto/32 is allowed to target itself.

quiz.question: Switch payload targets are relative to which address?
options: The start of the payload table
quiz.explanation: Both payload formats document their targets as relative to the switch opcode, not to the table that contains them.

quiz.question: What happens here when v0 is 7?
quiz.code:
sparse-switch v0, :sswitch_data
const/4 v1, 0x0
return v1
:case_ten
const/4 v1, 0x1
return v1
:sswitch_data
.sparse-switch
    0xa -> :case_ten
.end sparse-switch
options: Execution falls through to the instruction after sparse-switch
The verifier rejects the method because 7 has no case
It jumps to :case_ten, the nearest key
quiz.explanation: 7 matches no key, so the switch simply continues with the next instruction: v1 becomes 0 and is returned. Compilers put the default case right after the switch.

quiz.question: Which instruction does NOT end a basic block?
quiz.explanation: Arithmetic falls straight through to the next instruction. Jumps, returns and throws transfer control, so the following instruction starts a new block.

lessons.title: Annotations
lessons.summary: Read and write .annotation blocks: the build, runtime and system visibilities, the dalvik.annotation metadata that carries generics, throws clauses and inner-class information, parameter annotations, and the smali syntax for arrays, enums and nested annotations.

sections.title: Three visibilities
sections.body:
Every annotation in a dex file has a visibility byte:
- build (0x00): meant only for build-time tools. It matches Java's RetentionPolicy.CLASS, is not visible through reflection, and dexers commonly drop it.
- runtime (0x01): visible to reflection, e.g. getAnnotation(). Matches RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME.
- system (0x02): visible to the runtime but not to ordinary user annotation queries. Used for the dalvik.annotation.* metadata that replaces JVM class-file attributes.

Annotations with RetentionPolicy.SOURCE never reach the dex file at all.

sections.title: Class and method annotations
System annotations
sections.body:
javac class-file attributes become system annotations in dex:
- Signature: the generic signature of a class, field or method, stored as an array of strings that must be concatenated. It is not verified by the runtime and exists for reflection.
- Throws: the Class[] of a method's declared exceptions.
- EnclosingClass: the class lexically containing a member class (or an anonymous class outside any method).
- EnclosingMethod: the method containing a local or anonymous class. A class never has both EnclosingClass and EnclosingMethod, and either one requires InnerClass.
- InnerClass: the original simple name (null for anonymous classes) and declared access flags.
- MemberClasses: on the outer class, the list of its named member classes.
- MethodParameters: names and flags (0x10 final, 0x1000 synthetic, 0x8000 mandated) of a method's formal parameters. It was added after Android 7.1 and is ignored on older releases.
- AnnotationDefault: on an annotation interface, the default values of its elements.

sections.title: Metadata of a static nested class
Equivalent Java
Writing annotation values
sections.body:
Annotation element values use a small literal syntax:
- numbers, booleans, chars and strings as usual (0x2, true, 'a', "text"),
- types (Ljava/lang/String;), field and method references,
- arrays in braces: value = { "a", "b" },
- enum constants: .enum Lpkg/Kind;->FAST:Lpkg/Kind;
- nested annotations: .subannotation Lpkg/Tag; ... .end subannotation

Parameter annotations live inside a .param block attached to the parameter register, e.g. .param p1, "name" followed by its .annotation entries and .end param.

sections.title: An annotation type with a default
Missing annotations after R8
sections.body: Shrinkers remove metadata they consider unused. If an app relies on generic types or annotations at runtime (serialization libraries are typical), R8 must be told to keep them, for example with -keepattributes Signature,RuntimeVisibleAnnotations; otherwise those annotations are simply absent from the smali you read.

exercises.prompt: Write a method close()V (instance, empty body) whose Java declaration is void close() throws IOException, InterruptedException.
exercises.hint: Throws holds a Class[] array written with braces.

exercises.prompt: Annotate a String parameter of setName(Ljava/lang/String;)V with the build-time annotation Landroidx/annotation/NonNull;.
exercises.starterCode:
.method public setName(Ljava/lang/String;)V
    .registers 2
    return-void
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method public setName(Ljava/lang/String;)V
    .registers 2
    .param p1, "name"    # Ljava/lang/String;
        .annotation build Landroidx/annotation/NonNull;
        .end annotation
    .end param
    return-void
.end method
exercises.hint: In an instance method p0 is this, so the String is p1.

exercises.prompt: An anonymous Runnable is created inside Lcom/acme/demo/Task;->run()V. Which system annotations will its class carry, and what will they contain?
exercises.solution:
EnclosingMethod with value = Lcom/acme/demo/Task;->run()V (not EnclosingClass, because it is
defined inside a method), and InnerClass with name = null because the class is anonymous, plus
its accessFlags. The outer class does not list it in MemberClasses, which only contains named
member classes.
exercises.hint: Anonymous classes have no simple name, and EnclosingClass/EnclosingMethod are mutually exclusive.

quiz.question: Which visibility does dalvik.annotation.Signature use?
quiz.explanation: All dalvik.annotation.* metadata uses VISIBILITY_SYSTEM: readable by the runtime to implement reflection, not returned as an ordinary annotation.

quiz.question: Which two system annotations can never appear on the same class?
quiz.explanation: A class is scoped either by another class or by a method. Whichever applies, it must also carry InnerClass.

quiz.question: Can app code read this annotation with Class.getAnnotation() at runtime?
options: Yes, runtime visibility is exposed through reflection
No, only build tools can see it
Only if the class is also annotated with InnerClass
quiz.explanation: runtime corresponds to RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME and is the visibility reflection reports. build is for tools only, and system is reserved for runtime metadata.

quiz.question: What does name = null in a dalvik.annotation.InnerClass annotation mean?
options: The name was stripped by R8
quiz.explanation: InnerClass.name is the originally declared simple name; the format defines it as null for anonymous classes.

quiz.question: How is a generic signature stored in a Signature annotation?
options: As an array of strings that are concatenated
As a type_list in the proto
As debug info attached to the method
quiz.explanation: Splitting the signature into an array lets the pieces be shared with existing strings in the file. Readers concatenate the parts to get the full signature.

quiz.question: What happens to a Java annotation declared with RetentionPolicy.SOURCE?
options: It is discarded by the compiler and never appears in the dex
It is stored in the debug info
quiz.explanation: SOURCE annotations are dropped by javac or kotlinc and never reach the class files, so the dexer has nothing to convert.

lessons.title: Register Allocation
lessons.summary: Why compiled Smali uses the register numbers it does: how D8 assigns Java locals to registers, reuses them across live ranges, keeps parameters at the top of the frame, and inserts move/from16 shuffles when an instruction can only address v0-v15.

sections.title: Frames, parameters and the allocator
sections.body:
Every Dalvik method runs in a frame of registers_size registers. The last ins_size registers hold the incoming arguments (with `this` first for instance methods); everything below them is free for local values and temporaries. Smali's p-names are simply aliases for those top registers, so in a method with .registers 6 and two argument words, p0 is v4 and p1 is v5.

Java source variables do not map one-to-one onto registers. javac assigns local variable slots for the JVM, but D8 (and the older dx tool before it) rebuilds the code in its own intermediate form and runs a register allocator over it. D8 uses a linear-scan allocator: it computes how long each value is live and packs values whose live ranges do not overlap into the same register.

sections.title: Two temporaries, then reuse
sections.body:
.method public static sumOfSquares(II)I
    .registers 4

    mul-int v0, p0, p0
    mul-int v1, p1, p1
    add-int/2addr v0, v1
    return v0
.end method

sections.title: Equivalent Java
Why 4-bit formats shape the output
sections.body:
Many instruction formats store register numbers in 4 bits, which means they can only name v0-v15:
- 12x (move vA, vB, the /2addr arithmetic forms, array-length),
- 22c (iget/iput, instance-of, new-array),
- 22t (if-eq, if-lt and the other two-register comparisons),
- 35c (invoke-* and filled-new-array with up to five argument registers).

When a value the method needs lives in a higher register, the compiler has two options: copy it down first with a wider move (move/from16, move-object/from16 and move-wide/from16 use the 22x format: an 8-bit destination and a 16-bit source), or, for calls, use a /range invoke (format 3rc) whose arguments must be consecutive registers. The allocator therefore tries to give the busiest values low numbers, and large methods often begin by shuffling parameters into low registers.

sections.title: A parameter shuffle in a large frame
sections.body:
.method public describe()Ljava/lang/String;
    .registers 18

    # 17 locals (v0..v16), so `this` is p0 = v17 and cannot appear in a 22c iget.
    move-object/from16 v0, p0
    iget-object v1, v0, Lcom/acme/demo/User;->name:Ljava/lang/String;
    return-object v1
.end method

sections.title: One register, two variables
sections.body:
.method public static report(II)V
    .registers 3
    .param p0, "count"    # I
    .param p1, "limit"    # I

    .line 5
    sub-int v0, p1, p0
    .local v0, "remaining":I
    .line 6
    invoke-static {v0}, Lcom/acme/demo/Console;->print(I)V
    .end local v0    # "remaining":I

    .line 8
    mul-int/lit8 v0, p0, 0x2
    .local v0, "doubled":I
    .line 9
    invoke-static {v0}, Lcom/acme/demo/Console;->print(I)V

    .line 10
    return-void
.end method

sections.title: Reading .local and .end local
sections.body: Debug info tells you which source variable a register holds at each point. A .local directive starts a variable's range in that register and .end local closes it. When you see the same vN announced with different names, the allocator reused it because the two live ranges never overlapped. Release builds processed by R8 usually drop .local entries, so you have to track the values yourself.

sections.title: Editing register counts
sections.body: When you add a local to hand-edited Smali, raise .registers (or .locals). With .registers, that also moves every p-register up by one, so always refer to arguments by their p-names; code that hard-codes the old v-number of a parameter silently reads the wrong value.

exercises.prompt: This instance method has .registers 20 and one int parameter, so `this` is p0 = v18 and the int is p1 = v19. The iget-object below does not assemble because 22c only encodes v0-v15. Fix it without changing .registers.
exercises.hint: move-object/from16 (format 22x) can read any register up to v65535 and write v0-v255. Copy `this` into a low register first; the same register can then receive the field value.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite this method so it uses the smallest possible frame. It should still return p0 + p1 + p2.
exercises.starterCode:
.method public static sum3(III)I
    .registers 6
    add-int v0, p0, p1
    add-int v1, v0, p2
    return v1
.end method
exercises.solution:
.method public static sum3(III)I
    .registers 4
    add-int v0, p0, p1
    add-int/2addr v0, p2
    return v0
.end method
exercises.hint: The intermediate sum is dead as soon as the final sum is computed, so one local register is enough. add-int/2addr accumulates into its first operand.

quiz.question: In this method, which register is p1?
quiz.explanation: The arguments need 3 words (an int plus a two-register long), so they occupy v3-v5. p0 is v3 and the long p1 is the pair v4/v5, addressed by its first register, v4.

quiz.question: Why does D8 emit move-object/from16 v0, p0 before an iget-object in a method with 20 registers?
options: iget-object uses format 22c, whose register fields are only 4 bits wide
Fields can only be read through v0
It is required to null-check the object
quiz.explanation: In format 22c both register operands are nibbles, so only v0-v15 can be named. With 20 registers, p0 is v19 and must be copied into a low register first.

quiz.question: What does it tell you when debug info shows `.local v2, "i":I` and later `.local v2, "name":Ljava/lang/String;`?
options: The allocator reused v2 because the two variables' live ranges do not overlap
v2 is a wide register pair
The string is converted from the int
quiz.explanation: Registers are reused freely across non-overlapping live ranges, even with different types. The verifier tracks the type per instruction, so this is perfectly legal.

quiz.question: A call needs six argument registers. Which form must the compiler use?
quiz.explanation: Format 35c holds at most five argument registers. Six or more argument words require invoke-*/range, which takes a first register and a count, so the arguments must sit in a contiguous block.

quiz.question: Which format does move/from16 use?
quiz.explanation: 22x: an 8-bit destination (vAA) and a 16-bit source (vBBBB). move/16 uses 32x, with 16 bits for both registers.

lessons.title: Modern Android Instructions
lessons.summary: Method handles, call sites and the instructions that use them: invoke-polymorphic, invoke-custom, const-method-handle and const-method-type. Plus how D8 desugaring turns lambdas, string concatenation and interface methods into Smali that runs on older devices.

sections.title: Which DEX version brought what
sections.body:
The original Dalvik instruction set (DEX version 035) has no notion of java.lang.invoke. Later DEX versions added it in two steps:
- DEX 038 (Android 8.0, API 26) added invoke-polymorphic and invoke-custom, plus the method handle and call site sections of the file.
- DEX 039 (Android 9, API 28) added const-method-handle and const-method-type.

(DEX 037, Android 7.0, sits in between and only added support for default interface methods.) A runtime refuses DEX files whose version is newer than it understands, which is why D8 picks the file version from your minSdk and only emits these instructions when the minimum API allows it.

sections.title: Method handle constants and a polymorphic call
sections.body:
